## Abstract

Collective modes in Fermi liquids are usually regarded as dissipation channels that relax electronic excitations through Landau damping. Whether such modes can instead mediate the formation of correlated electronic states under non-equilibrium conditions remains an open question. Here, we show that under optical photo-doping, a bulk plasmon can drive correlated inter-band transfer within a transient electronic continuum. Using time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (Tr-ARPES) on $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ supported by electronic structure calculations, we observe that at high excitation density, plasmons transfer energy from a weakly dispersing bulk band into unoccupied surface states. This bulk-to-surface redistribution stabilizes a long-lived, energy-localized spectral feature consistent with a Mahan exciton. Our results reveal a non-equilibrium regime of Fermi-liquid physics in which collective modes do not merely dissipate energy, but also stabilize correlated bound states.

Collective excitations in interacting Fermi systems are traditionally regarded as decay channels. In a conventional Fermi liquid, the plasmon branch lies outside the particle–hole continuum at long wavelengths, but enters it at finite momentum, where Landau damping transfers plasmon energy into electron–hole pairs (Fig. 1a) [Nozieres2018TheLiquids, Wehling2014DiracMaterials]. This paradigm underlies the standard description of relaxation in metals, where collective modes redistribute electronic energy into particle–hole continua.

Such relaxation also extends to non-equilibrium settings: in optically excited metals and semiconductors, bosonic-mode-assisted inter- and intra-band scattering channels have been directly observed transferring high-energy carriers into lower-energy electronic continua and bound states [Na2019DirectDomain, Schmitt2022FormationTime, Madeo2020]. Moreover, transient excitonic states are suppressed in metals when the dephasing of plasmons screens the electron-hole Coulomb interaction [Cui2014TransientSurfaces]. In these cases, collective modes function as an efficient pathway toward equilibration. Yet this established framework leaves open the fundamental question of whether collective modes, rather than merely dissipating energy, can also actively drive excitations of a particle-hole continuum, and generate correlated electronic states under non-equilibrium conditions.

In general, inter-band optical excitation generates a non-equilibrium carrier population that rapidly thermalizes to a secondary chemical potential within transiently filled bands [Gierz2013SnapshotsGraphene]. The resulting inter- and intra-band excitation continua can extend to $\omega=0$ , overlapping with the plasmon branch (Fig. 1b). In this regime, collective modes need not act solely as sinks of energy; they may instead mediate inter-band transfer within the transient continuum.

Observing such an interaction channel in a bulk metal, however, is challenging. In 3D systems, strong screening and the large phase space tend to smear interaction-enhanced features. Plasmons are heavily damped once they overlap with bulk continua, and competing scattering channels redistribute spectral weight broadly in momentum and energy. A more favorable setting would involve 2D surface electronic bands interacting with the bulk plasmon of a 3D system. The reduced dimensionality of the surface suppresses phase space, weakens screening, and therefore enhances interaction effects. Moreover, the near-field interaction between the dipole moment of a bulk collective mode in a low-carrier-density material and surface-localized conduction electrons is exponentially enhanced at zero-momentum transfer [Lee2014InterfacialSrTiO3]. In this configuration, a bulk plasmon could hence transfer energy to the more confined surface electron bands, giving rise to correlated features that can be spectrally resolved.

In this work, we experimentally and theoretically demonstrate that $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ precisely provides the latter setting – we observe that the electronic structure of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ hosts a bulk plasmon at an energy scale comparable to the separation between an unoccupied, weakly dispersing bulk band and an unoccupied surface state. Our density-functional theory (DFT) calculations establish the existence of these unoccupied surface states, motivating the experimental investigation of plasmon-mediated transfer between the bulk and surface in the non-equilibrium continuum. Using time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (Tr-ARPES), we not only directly demonstrate this plasmon-mediated transfer, but also find that the reduced screening and constrained phase space of the surface potentially stabilizes a long-lived, energy-localized spectral feature consistent with a Mahan exciton [Mahan1967ExcitonsSemiconductors, Mahan1967ExcitonsMass, Asnin1983CoulombGermanium, Palmieri2020MahanPerovskites]. Our results reveal a non-equilibrium regime of Fermi-liquid physics in which collective modes do not simply dissipate energy, but also actively reshape electronic distributions by driving bulk-to-surface transfer and generating electronic bound states.

$\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ has previously been characterized as semiconducting [Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor, Nelson2024RevealingLa-Doping, Shi2024AbsenceEffect] or semimetallic [Ma2019SpinEuCd2As2, Roychowdhury2023AnomalousEuCd2As2] throughout its magnetic phase diagram (Supplementary Material (SM) Sec. I [2026SeeURL]), with an antiferromagnetic phase reported below $T_{N}=$9\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ . In the samples used in this work, ferromagnetic (FM) order has been stabilized below $T_{C}=$25\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ through Eu vacancies [Roychowdhury2023AnomalousEuCd2As2]. Above $T_{C}$ , $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ lies in a paramagnetic (PM) state with bulk inversion ( $\mathcal{I}$ ) and time-reversal ( $\mathcal{T}$ ) symmetries. To analyze the bulk and surface spectra of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ , we performed DFT and Wannier-based tight-binding calculations of the electronic structure (SM Sec. III.1 [2026SeeURL]). Because our ARPES measurements produced qualitatively identical spectra both above and below $T_{C}$ over the energy and momentum range probed in this study (SM Sec. II [2026SeeURL]), we performed our DFT calculations in the PM state. Our DFT calculations reveal unoccupied $(001)$ -surface bands that coexist with the projected continuum of unoccupied bulk states (the projected bulk conduction manifold) and exhibit an approximately hyperbolic dispersion with an energy minimum that we denote as $\widetilde{E}$ (Fig. 2a, see SM Sec. III.2 [2026SeeURL]). Through calculations of the $(001)$ -surface spin texture in SM Sec. III.3 [2026SeeURL], we find that the $(001)$ -surface states form a 2D Dirac cone with weak spin-orbit-coupling- (SOC-) driven splitting away from ${\bf k}={\bf 0}$ .

To understand the origin of the hyperbolic $(001)$ -surface Dirac cone, we applied the group-theoretic methodology in Ref. [Vergniory2022AllMaterials] to compute the band topology at and away from $E_{F}$ (SM Sec. III.4 [2026SeeURL]). We identified a large range of electronic fillings – spanning from 5 electrons below intrinsic filling to 7 electrons above – at which $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ in the PM state hosts 3D topological band-insulating gaps. We may therefore associate the unoccupied $(001)$ -surface states in Fig. 2a to a 3D topological band insulator phase at an electronic filling above $E_{F}$ , which can be accessed by photo-doping experiments. In this sense, $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ is reminiscent of the repeat-topological materials introduced in Ref. [Vergniory2022AllMaterials] (e.g. $\text{Bi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{Mg}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}$ [Chang2019RealizationMg3Bi2, Zhou2019ExperimentalEpitaxy]), which host topological gaps at and just below $E_{F}$ . The unoccupied $(001)$ -surface states in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ and the associated topological band gaps above $E_{F}$ can hence be viewed as a generalization of the concept of repeat-topology to topological surface conduction bands that are accessible by doping and Tr-ARPES experiments like those in the present study.

Having established the presence and energies of unoccupied surface states in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ , we now use Tr-ARPES to dynamically populate and resolve the surface bands. In our measurements, p-polarized IR pulses at either $1.2\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ or $1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ excite inter-band transitions, after which we collect ARPES spectra using $6\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ photons with a variable delay from photo-excitation. In momentum space, the photon scattering plane coincides with a crystallographic mirror plane whose normal vector lies along $k_{y}$ and is related to the Brillouin zone line $\overline{\Gamma}-\overline{\mathrm{K}}$ in Fig. 2a by crystal symmetry. In Fig. 2b, we show an ARPES spectrum ( $E$ vs $k_{y}$ ) of the occupied and unoccupied bulk and surface band structure of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ . Below $E_{F}$ (i.e. at energies $E-E_{0}<$-0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ , where $E_{0}$ is assigned to the bottom of a bright electron-like unoccupied band), a broad valence band is visible, consistent with equilibrium synchrotron ARPES measurements [Roychowdhury2023AnomalousEuCd2As2] and the bulk DFT calculations performed in the present study (gray lines, see SM Sec. III.1 [2026SeeURL]).

Around $0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ above $E_{F}$ in Fig. 2b ( $\emph{i.e.}$ above $E_{0}$ ), we observe a sharp, nearly-linear (hyperbolic) electron-like feature, in strong agreement with the Wannier model surface spectral function in Fig. 2a. Next, at $E_{CBM}\equiv E_{0}-$0.12\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ in Fig. 2b, we observe a faint incoherent spectral weight that we attribute to a weakly dispersing bulk conduction band $0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ above $E_{F}$ , consistent with optical spectroscopy [Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor, Wu2024TheSingularity] and high-energy electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) measurements (SM Sec. V [2026SeeURL]), as well as our bulk DFT calculations (SM Sec. III.1 [2026SeeURL]). In Fig. 2c, we show circular dichroism (CD-) ARPES measurements of the $(001)$ -surface states, which provide further details of their wavefunction textures, and exhibit excellent agreement with theoretical calculations of the surface-projected local (in real space) atomic-orbital contribution to the orbital angular momentum (Fig. 2d, see SM Sec. III.3 [2026SeeURL]).

We next investigate the dynamics of the photo-doped surface and bulk conduction bands under different photo-excitation fluences. In Fig. 3a, we plot ARPES spectra at several different time delays after excitation for representative cases of low ( $15\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ , top) and high ( $55\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ , bottom) fluences (SM Sec. VIII.3 [2026SeeURL]). Immediately after excitation, a broad energy range is populated at both low and high fluence (left panels of the top and bottom rows of Fig. 3a, respectively). The photo-doped population above $E_{F}$ (here, in the vicinity of the bottom of the surface band $E_{0}$ , see Fig. 2b) corresponds to the non-equilibrium phase depicted in Fig. 1b. At low fluence, only states in the nondispersing bulk conduction band ( $E\approx E_{CBM}<E_{0}$ ) remain occupied several picoseconds after excitation (Fig. 3a, top right). This is consistent with previous studies that mapped the unoccupied band structure in solids [Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor, Gierz2013SnapshotsGraphene, Puppin2022Excited-stateMapping, Bao2022PopulationCd3As2, Fragkos2024Excited1T-ZrTe2], in which long-lived populations above $E_{F}$ were associated with the energy minima of unoccupied bulk bands. At negative delays, we faintly resolve a non-equilibrium energy-localized population distribution, induced by photon-energy-dependent direct inter-band excitations (SM Sec. IV [2026SeeURL]). At and after $t_{0}$ , the momentum-integrated population at different times (Fig. 3b, left panel) can be fit using Fermi-Dirac distributions multiplied by linear densities of states (SM Sec. VI [2026SeeURL]). We find that the resulting chemical potential at later delay times $\mu(t\gg t_{0})$ is largely independent of fluence, and that $\mu(t\gg t_{0})\approx$100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$+E_{0}$ for $1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ photon excitation. Such cooling is largely consistent with a two-temperature model in which photo-excitation raises the temperature of electrons, which then cool by transferring energy to a bath of collective bosonic modes, such as phonons, magnons, or plasmons (see SM Sec. VIII.2 [2026SeeURL] for further details).

Surprisingly, at high fluence (Fig. 3a, bottom row), a strong spectral weight persists at $E_{X}\equiv E_{0}+$100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ , significantly above the surface band minimum $E_{0}$ (SM Sec. VII [2026SeeURL]), even after the populations at lower energies have largely decayed (Fig. 3a, bottom right). The strong energy localization of this long-lived spectral weight, and its qualitative absence for low fluence excitation, are shown in Fig. 3b. A clear transfer of spectral weight to lower energies over several picoseconds is visible for low fluence excitation (Fig. 3b, left), whereas for high fluence excitation (Fig. 3b, right), the spectrum after $t_{0}$ remains distinctly sharpened at $E_{X}$ relative to the initial hot electron distribution.

To identify the origin of the long-lived population at $E_{X}$ in Fig. 3, we next examine the role of many-body interactions in the unoccupied bands. Under low fluence excitation, the imaginary part of the self energy $\text{Im }\Sigma(E)$ extracted from ARPES linewidths [Kaminski2005OnSpectroscopy] (SM Secs. VI and VII [2026SeeURL]) shows a strong discontinuity in its derivative (a “kink”) at $E-E_{0}\approx$200\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ (Fig. 4a). Under non-equilibrium distributions in weakly interacting systems, such kinks can arise from changes in quasiparticle lifetimes due to crossovers in phase-space-allowed scattering mechanisms [duvel], and therefore here indicate strong coupling of the surface states in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ to a collective mode with the corresponding energy. Previous optical spectroscopy experiments [Wang2016AnisotropicProperties] and EELS measurements at equilibrium performed in this work (Fig. 4b) identify the relevant mode between $0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ and $0.2\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ above $E_{0}$ as the bulk plasmon. This suggests that, although the surface conduction band dynamics in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ differ sharply from previous Tr-ARPES studies of conduction band dynamics in a broad set of materials [Sobota2013DirectBi2Se3, Sobota2014UltrafastSpectroscopy, Tanimura2015UltrafastSpectroscopy, Puppin2022Excited-stateMapping] – in which electron-electron scattering is the dominant interaction far from $E_{F}$ – the low fluence conduction band dynamics in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ can still be understood with a conventional two-temperature model in which a cold bath of bosons (here plasmons) provides a relaxation channel for hot electrons (see SM Sec. VIII.2 [2026SeeURL] and Refs. [Allen1987TheoryMetals, Sun2012DynamicsGraphene, Gierz2014Non-equilibriumSpectroscopy, Bao2022PopulationCd3As2]).

However at high fluence excitation, we posit that the role of plasmons is qualitatively different. We specifically instead propose that in the high-fluence regime, the persistence of localized spectral weight at $E_{X}$ arises due to a hot plasmon-driven inter-band transition that drives electrons from the bulk conduction band just below $E_{0}$ (yellow triangle in Fig. 2b) to states at $E_{X}$ in the surface conduction band. This process corresponds precisely to the interaction between the plasmon branch and the non-equilibrium particle-hole continuum in Fig. 1b. Under high excitation fluence, a Mahan exciton may then form from the Coulomb interaction of the electron-hole pairs (schematically depicted in Fig. 5a).

Mahan excitons specifically form with electrons at the effective Fermi level of an n-doped system when hole densities are negligible due to valence degeneracy [Mahan1967ExcitonsSemiconductors, Mahan1967ExcitonsMass]. In support of this scenario in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ , we previously noted that the chemical potential $\mu$ of the population in the unoccupied surface bands cools to $\mu(t\gg t_{0})\approx E_{0}+$100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ (SM Sec. VI [2026SeeURL]), which is equal to $E_{X}$ . Moreover, our assessment of high valence degeneracy is supported by optical spectroscopy studies, which identify a bulk conduction band with a large mass at $\Gamma$ in the energy range of the yellow triangle at $E_{CBM}$ in Fig. 2b [Wu2024TheSingularity, Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor], as well as our PM-state DFT calculations, which show a doubly degenerate bulk band at approximately the same energy that is flat to leading order in 3D $k$ -space near $\Gamma$ (SM Sec. III.1 [2026SeeURL]).

To test the interpretation of a Mahan exciton at high fluence excitation, we first search for signatures of holes in the bulk conduction band after photo-excitation. This is challenging, because at equilibrium, all of the bulk and surface states participating in this scenario are unoccupied. To identify holes in the bulk conduction band, we therefore compare population dynamics between the excitonic and non-excitonic conditions, which in our experiments respectively correspond to high ( $55\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ ) and low ( $15\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ ) fluence excitation. In Fig. 5b, we show the difference between time traces taken at high and low fluence, with the maximum spectral weight at each energy for both fluences normalized to one after subtracting a pre- $t_{0}$ background signal (see SM Sec. VIII [2026SeeURL] for a detailed description and justification of the background subtraction and normalization procedure). Strikingly, a relative depletion of spectral weight for high fluence accumulates at $E_{CBM}\equiv E_{0}-$100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ during the first $2\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$ (dark blue region in Fig. 5b). This indicates that the initial population decay at $E_{CBM}$ is faster for high fluence excitation than at low fluence. Simultaneously, a substantially larger relative spectral weight at high fluence accumulates at $E_{X}$ within a few picoseconds (gold region in Fig. 5b), consistent with the longer lifetime of an excitonic population.

We interpret these observations as evidence for an additional process – apparent only at high fluence – that transfers spectral weight across the inter-band transition from $E_{CBM}$ to $E_{X}$ (blue arrow in Fig. 5b) over the corresponding $2\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$ timescale. The energy difference $E_{X}-E_{CBM}$ is approximately equal to the plasmon energy previously identified in Fig. 4, strongly suggesting that the transfer is plasmon-induced. In turn, the rate of such plasmon absorption should scale quadratically with the excited carrier density, because the plasmons must first be excited by the relaxation of electrons that were themselves previously excited into the unoccupied bands in a system that started at low temperature. Hence, the plasmon-induced transition from $E_{CBM}$ to $E_{X}$ is only dominant at high fluence, and excitons should not form in the low-fluence regime, consistent with our observations in Fig. 3a.

The onset of such a second-order process should also be continuous: at low fluences (including $15\text{\,}\mathrm{u}\mathrm{J}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{c}\mathrm{m}^{2}$ ), plasmon-induced transitions would be negligible, but not strictly forbidden. Consistent with this expectation, we observe a crossover from the low-fluence to high-fluence regime at approximately $46\text{\,}\mathrm{u}\mathrm{J}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{c}\mathrm{m}^{2}$ (SM Secs. VI and VIII.3 [2026SeeURL]). Specifically, at this intermediate fluence, we can resolve the initial thermalization of the hot electron distribution – due to a relatively small population of plasmon-driven electron-hole pairs compared to hot electrons (SM Sec. VI [2026SeeURL]) – while simultaneously resolving a relative dearth of electron accumulation near $E_{CBM}$ immediately after excitation (SM Sec. VIII.3 [2026SeeURL]). For completeness, we additionally note that in Fig. 5b, a relative dearth of electrons for high fluence excitation is also present around $E_{CBM}$ at later delay times ( $t-t_{0}>$6\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$$ ). We attribute this long-lived dearth of electrons at $E_{CBM}$ – the relative intensity of which shows fluence dependence (SM Sec. VIII.4 [2026SeeURL]) – to a persisting population in the conduction band that is larger at low fluence. Importantly, however, this long-lived conduction band population evolves over slower timescales, and hence does not influence our proposed mechanism of plasmon-driven electron-hole pair formation.

The contrast between the dynamics at low and high excitation fluence can be captured using a modified rate equation that models the photo-excited population as relaxing via plasmon-mediated scattering through an additional channel that at high fluence transfers spectral weight between electron and hole energies upon the formation of excitons. A detailed description of the model is provided in SM Sec. VIII.2 [2026SeeURL]. In Fig. 5c, we show numerical data generated using this theoretical model, which are in close agreement with the experimental data in Fig. 5b. We obtained the input parameters for the theoretical model through independent fits of Tr-ARPES time traces at low and high fluence. The model parameters respectively indicate an exciton formation time and lifetime of approximately $1.4\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$ and $4.4\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$ , though with moderate correlation between the two values. Lastly, in SM Sec. IX [2026SeeURL], we discuss in detail alternative, non-excitonic interpretations of the fluence-dependent electron dynamics in our experimental data, and ultimately find these alternative scenarios to be inconsistent with our complete dataset.

To conclude, the signatures of Mahan excitons in our measurements motivate future studies to probe their spin polarization [Mori2023Spin-polarizedInsulator], electronic chirality [Kung2019ObservationBi2Se3], condensation [Pertsova2018ExcitonicMaterials, Mori2025PossibleInsulator], and tunable binding energies [Pertsova2018ExcitonicMaterials]. From a broader perspective, our results point to a generalized form of carrier multiplication, in which the absorption of a photon creates multiple electron-hole excitations [Nozik2009Nanophotonics:Photons]. Moreover, due to the coherent near-field coupling to bulk modes demonstrated in this study, surface non-equilibrium Fermi liquids constitute a powerful platform for inducing collective interaction-driven phenomena that are otherwise inaccessible at thermal equilibrium, including phononic control of phase transitions [Rini2007ControlExcitation, Basov2017TowardsMaterials] and intrinsically driven Floquet phases [Hubener2018PhononMatter].

### Time- and Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy Measurements

The Tr-ARPES experiments were performed in the home lab at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign. The fifth harmonic ( $6\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ ) of the $1.2\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ ( $1030\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$ ) output of a Yb:KGW amplified laser (Pharos, Light Conversion) was used as the probe. The linearly polarized probe was transmitted through a quarter waveplate for CD-ARPES measurements. The IR excitation pulses of $1.2\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ ( $1000\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$ ) and $1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ ( $825\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$ ) were provided by an OPA (Orpheus, Light Conversion) pumped by the same Yb:KGW laser. Measurements were performed using a hemispherical analyzer (DA-30L, Scienta Omicron) equipped with a deflection mode to observe dispersion along both in-plane axes without rotation of the sample. The geometry of the Tr-ARPES experiment is shown in Fig. 6. The sample crystal axes were aligned using the measured Fermi surface. ### First-Principles and Surface State Calculations

We performed the ab initio calculations of the electronic structure of the PM phase of EuCd2As2 within the density-functional theory (DFT) framework, as implemented in the Quantum Espresso software package [Giannozzi2009QUANTUMMaterials, Giannozzi2017AdvancedESPRESSO, Giannozzi2020QuantumExascale]. The calculations included fully relativistic spin–orbit coupling (SOC) in the noncollinear scheme. In this setup, when no initial magnetic moments are specified, the self-consistent cycle converges to a nonmagnetic, time-reversal- ( $\mathcal{T}$ -) invariant solution. To properly localize the half-filled Eu $4f$ orbitals and improve the overall accuracy of the PM-state band structure, a Hubbard $U$ correction of $U=5$ eV on the Eu sites was implemented within the GGA $+\ U$ scheme [Dudarev1998Electron-energy-lossStudy]. To analyze the spectral and topological properties of the PM state, we used maximally localized Wannier functions [Pizzi2020Wannier90Applications, Marzari1997MaximallyBands, Souza2001MaximallyBands] to construct a tight-binding model using the Eu 5d and 4f, Cd 5s, and As 4p orbitals with SOC, and symmetrized the model [Zhi2022WannSymm:Orbitals] using the crystal symmetries in space group 164 ( $P$ $\bar{3}m1$ ) and $\mathcal{T}$ symmetry. To study the $(001)$ -surface states, we constructed a finite slab model using the PythTB software package [PythTB] with the Wannier model as input. Within the slab model, we then computed the surface spectral function and spin and orbital angular momentum textures using surface Green’s functions (see SM Sec. III [2026SeeURL] for complete DFT calculation details).

### Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy Measurements

To increase the scattering intensity for momentum-resolved electron energy loss spectroscopy (M-EELS) measurements, five single crystals of $\text{FM}\text{\hskip 1.29167pt--\hskip 1.29167pt}\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ from the same batch used for the Tr-ARPES measurements were roughly vertically co-aligned on an oxygen-free, high-conductivity copper puck. The samples were secured with Ag-epoxy (EPOTEK H2OE) cured at 150°C for an hour. Custom posts were mounted on top of the samples using the same epoxy. After preparation, the samples were cleaved in a UHV chamber ( $\sim$ $5\text{\times}{10}^{-10}\text{\,}\mathrm{T}\mathrm{o}\mathrm{r}\mathrm{r}$ ) at room temperature and transferred into the M-EELS measurement chamber held at $\sim$ $7\text{\times}{10}^{-11}\text{\,}\mathrm{T}\mathrm{o}\mathrm{r}\mathrm{r}$ .

The M-EELS experiments were performed in a reflection geometry using a modified high-resolution EELS spectrometer (ELS5000, LK Technologies) with the sample placed in an eucentric cryogenic three-circle goniometer [Vig2017MeasurementM-EELS]. Samples were placed such that the out-of-plane momentum transfer was along the c-axis. An incident energy of $50\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ with an energy resolution of $6.6\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ was used. Due to the rough alignment of the individual crystals, the momentum in the scattering plane was considered integrated (i.e., a single value of $q$ contains information summed over the full Brillouin zone).

### Sample Synthesis

The $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ samples were grown using a salt-flux method, with high-quality elemental Eu, Cd, and As pieces, and an equimolar ratio of NaCl and KCl. The growth method – as well as sample characterization through transport, scanning tunneling microscopy, and soft X-ray ARPES – are described in Ref. [Roychowdhury2023AnomalousEuCd2As2]. We note that the salt flux growth method used for the samples in this work (as opposed to the Sn flux method more commonly used for the growth of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ ) leads to an approximately $1\text{\,}\%$ concentration of Eu vacancies, which results in FM order appearing below $T_{C}\sim$25\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ (as opposed to antiferromagnetic ordering below $T_{N}\sim$9\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ ) [Jo2020ManipulatingEuCd2As2].

There has been much controversy [Ma2019SpinEuCd2As2, Jo2020ManipulatingEuCd2As2, Soh2019IdealExchange, Roychowdhury2023AnomalousEuCd2As2, Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor, Shi2024AbsenceEffect, Cuono2023AbCompounds, Nelson2024RevealingLa-Doping] surrounding the subject of whether the ferromagnetic (FM) state of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ is a topological Weyl semimetal or a gapped semiconductor. Here, we present experimental evidence that the samples used in this work are semimetallic in the FM phase.

Initial work on $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ described it as a Dirac semimetal above $100\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ (in the paramagnetic state), and argued that at intermediate temperatures, between $100\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ and the antiferromagnetic transition ( $T_{N}=$9\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ ), ferromagnetic fluctuations lead to magnetic splitting of the Dirac point into a pair of Weyl points [Ma2019SpinEuCd2As2]. In this scenario, the electronic band structure of the Weyl semimetal phase includes two pairs of band crossings with linear dispersion whose nodal degeneracies lie $50\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ above the Fermi energy ( $E_{F}$ ), as schematically depicted with blue and yellow bands in the right panel of Fig. S1a. We note that for clarity, only a single Weyl cone is schematically depicted in the right panel of Fig. S1a; the second Weyl cone is predicted to lie at the same energy but offset along the $k_{z}$ direction. The hole-like band (blue), as well as the splitting thereof under ferromagnetic fluctuations, was previously measured through synchrotron ARPES studies [Ma2019SpinEuCd2As2]. However, because it lies above $E_{F}$ , the electron-like band (yellow in Fig. S1a, right panel) could not be clearly resolved through the same measurements. Nevertheless, the dispersion of an electron-like band was faintly resolved using quasiparticle interference in scanning tunneling microscopy measurements [Roychowdhury2023AnomalousEuCd2As2]. Further experiments stabilized FM order below a transition temperature of $T_{C}=$25\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ through the introduction of Eu vacancies [Roychowdhury2023AnomalousEuCd2As2]; we use the same samples as in Ref. [Roychowdhury2023AnomalousEuCd2As2] (with Eu vacancies) in this work. Hence for the samples studied in this work, we expect the presence of bulk Weyl and (potentially massive) Dirac points respectively below and above $T_{C}=$25\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ .

However, several recent studies instead characterize $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ as a semiconductor [Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor, Cuono2023AbCompounds, Shi2024AbsenceEffect, Nelson2024RevealingLa-Doping], questioning the robustness of the semimetallic characterization of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ in the earlier works. The semiconducting electronic band structure proposed in these studies is schematically depicted in the left panel of Fig. S1a, and is based on the results of Tr-ARPES [Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor] and La-doping-supported ARPES [Nelson2024RevealingLa-Doping] experiments on samples grown with high-purity Eu. These measurements specifically identified a hole-like valence band with a maximum slightly above $E_{F}$ (in agreement with ARPES measurements that supported the Weyl semimetal characterization), as well as a conduction band minimum $0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{-}$ $0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ above $E_{F}$ , but did not show evidence of an electron-like band immediately above $E_{F}$ (the yellow band in the right panel of Fig. S1a). The semiconducting gap was further observed to be temperature-independent; neither the Weyl nor the Dirac semimetal phases were observed [Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor]. Nevertheless, we note that the existence of a large-mass conduction band $0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ - $0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ above $E_{F}$ (the green band in both panels of Fig. S1a) has been confirmed by previous experimental observation of a strong peak at the corresponding infrared absorption spectrum, both in samples characterized as semiconducting [Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor] and in those characterized as semimetallic [Wu2024TheSingularity].

Our static $6\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ laser ARPES measurements of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ , shown in Fig. S1b, corroborate equilibrium ARPES studies taken using X-ray probe photons, which unanimously report a hole-like valence band with a maximum near $E_{F}$ (for both semimetallic [Roychowdhury2023AnomalousEuCd2As2] and semiconducting [Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor] samples). However, our time-resolved (Tr-) ARPES experiments suggest that the samples analyzed in this study are semimetallic in the FM state via the observation of semimetallic thermodynamics.

Specifically, in Fig. S1c, we show the change in the spectral weight near $E_{F}$ at the instant of photo-excitation with $1.2\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ photons. We observe a transient increase in electronic occupation above $E_{F}$ (orange data points in Fig. S1c), accompanied by a decrease below $E_{F}$ (dark blue data points in Fig. S1c). Such broadening of the Fermi edge in response to photo-excitation is ubiquitous in Tr-ARPES experiments, and is generally interpreted as rapid heating of electrons by the pump pulse, followed by the slower cooling of electrons via coupling to phonons [Gierz2013SnapshotsGraphene]. The time trace in Fig. S1d shows electron distribution curves (EDCs) taken at various pump-probe delays for $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ under $1.2\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ photo-excitation at $T\approx T_{C}$ . At $t_{0}$ , as described earlier, there is a transient increase in population above $E_{F}$ , along with a faint decrease in occupation below $E_{F}$ ; these two disturbances cool over the following few picoseconds. In Fig. S1e, we demonstrate that the EDCs in Fig. S1d of hot electrons at various time delays are well-fit by Fermi-Dirac distributions multiplied by a parabolic density of states centered $50\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ above $E_{F}$ . The transient electronic temperature $T_{e}$ and chemical potential $\mu$ as functions of time extracted from the fits in Fig. S1e are shown in Fig. S1f. We find that the increase in electronic temperature in response to the pump pulse at $t=t_{0}$ is accompanied by a decrease in the extracted chemical potential. Moreover, the recovery of the electronic temperature to a quasi-equilibrium value is exponential, with a timescale ( $2.73\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$ ) approximately double that of the exponential recovery of the chemical potential ( $1.46\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$ ).

To interpret this result, we recall that the relation between the chemical potential and temperature for a (semi)metal or doped semiconductor can be derived through a Sommerfeld expansion: $\Delta\mu\propto-T^{2}g^{\prime}(E_{F})/g(E_{F})$ , where $g(E)$ is the density of states in energy [Ashcroft1976SolidPhysics]. Crucially, this indicates that for an inherently p-doped semiconductor – in which the density of states decreases with increasing energy – an increase (decrease) in chemical potential with increasing (decreasing) temperature is expected. However, for a charge-neutral semimetal (i.e. a semimetal with $E_{F}$ at the band crossing), the density of states increases with increasing energy, leading to an increase (decrease) in chemical potential with decreasing (increasing) temperature. We therefore assert that when the temperature of the electrons in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ is increased by the pump pulse, much of the increase in spectral weight above $E_{F}$ is realized above the Weyl point in an electron-like band, which leads to the transient decrease in $\mu$ and its subsequent recovery at twice the decay rate of $T$ . For comparison, previous Tr-ARPES experiments on strongly p-type graphene ( $E_{0}\approx E_{F}-0.2\,\mathrm{eV}$ ) show simultaneous increases in both $\mu$ and $T_{e}$ in response to photo-excitation [Gierz2013SnapshotsGraphene]. We also note that similar observations have been made in the 3D Dirac semimetal $\text{Cd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ [Bao2022PopulationCd3As2], and in the 2D Dirac surface states of the topological insulator $\text{Bi}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{Se}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}$ [Ponzoni2023DiracMicroscopy].

Finally, we note that the magnetism-induced splitting below $T_{C}$ does not affect the aforementioned arguments. Due to the large expected size of the splitting (on the order of $0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolAngstrom}$ ), we expect that Fig. S1b shows the dispersion of a single Weyl fermion. The theoretical description of the dynamics shown in Fig. S1f similarly remains unchanged when we account for the presence of a second Weyl point. Moreover, across all of the experimental analysis in this study, the emergence of magnetic ordering across $T_{C}$ does not significantly affect our observations, aside from shifting the plasmon energy (see the main text for further details).

Overall, though our data is consistent with the presence of a Weyl semimetal phase in the FM state, the phase diagram of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ – and the relative roles of magnetic impurities and Eu vacancies – are likely complex. $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ may feature both semiconducting and semimetallic regimes, and its magnetic and (topological) electronic phase diagrams consequently merit further study.

## III First-Principles Calculations

In this section we will perform and analyze ab initio density-functional theory (DFT) calculations and construct Wannier tight-binding models to study the bulk electronic structure, surface states, and band topology of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ . Because the ARPES measurements in this work produced qualitatively similar data both above and below the paramagnetic (PM) to FM transition temperature of $T_{c}\approx$25\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$$ (see Fig. S5 and Sec. II), we will focus our analysis below on the simpler case of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ in the PM state. We will first in Sec. III.1 detail our DFT calculations and the construction of our Wannier model. In Sec. III.2, we will then use surface Green’s functions in a finite slab Hamiltonian to obtain the $(001)$ - ( $\hat{z}$ -normal) surface spectrum of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ in the PM state, and quantify the contribution of the Eu $4f$ states to the surface spectrum, as they exert a strong influence on the surface chemical potential via the Hubbard $U$ parameter in our DFT calculations (Sec. III.1). Our analysis in Sec. III.2 reveals the presence of unoccupied $(001)$ -surface bands that coexist with the projected continuum of unoccupied bulk states (the projected bulk conduction manifold), consistent with our Tr-ARPES experiments (see Fig. 2b of the main text).

To further our understanding of the $(001)$ -surface states, we will next in Sec. III.3 compute the surface spin and orbital angular momentum (OAM) textures, which reveal the surface states to be a 2D Dirac cone with weak spin-orbit-coupling- (SOC-) driven splitting away from ${\bf k}={\bf 0}$ . We will also in Sec. III.3 introduce a simplified low-energy ${\bf k}\cdot{\bf p}$ Hamiltonian that qualitatively reproduces the dispersion and angular momentum textures of the $(001)$ -surface states obtained from our DFT-based calculations. Lastly, in Sec. III.4, we will apply the methods of Ref. [Vergniory2022AllMaterials] to our PM-state DFT calculation to analyze the band topology of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ at and away from $E_{F}$ . Through this analysis, we identify a large range of contiguous topological gaps in the bulk conduction manifold, from which we conclude that the unoccupied $(001)$ -surface bands in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ can be viewed as the 2D topological surface states of a 3D topological band insulator phase at an electronic filling above $E_{F}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{a}_{1} \displaystyle=(4.4499000\,\textnormal{\AA})\ \hat{\mathbf{x}}, \displaystyle\mathbf{a}_{2} \displaystyle=(-2.2249500\,\textnormal{\AA})\ \hat{\mathbf{x}}+(3.8537264\,\textnormal{\AA})\ \hat{\mathbf{y}}, \displaystyle\mathbf{a}_{3} \displaystyle=(7.3499999\,\textnormal{\AA})\ \hat{\mathbf{z}}. $$

The primitive reciprocal lattice vectors of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ are then correspondingly given by:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{b}_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{2\pi(\mathbf{a}_{2}\times\mathbf{a}_{3})}{\mathbf{a}_{1}\cdot(\mathbf{a}_{2}\times\mathbf{a}_{3})}=(1.41198348\,\textnormal{\AA}^{-1})\ \hat{\mathbf{x}}+(0.81520904\,\textnormal{\AA}^{-1})\ \hat{\mathbf{y}}, \displaystyle\mathbf{b}_{2} \displaystyle=\frac{2\pi(\mathbf{a}_{3}\times\mathbf{a}_{1})}{\mathbf{a}_{1}\cdot(\mathbf{a}_{2}\times\mathbf{a}_{3})}=(1.63041809\,\textnormal{\AA}^{-1})\ \hat{\mathbf{y}}, \displaystyle\mathbf{b}_{3} \displaystyle=\frac{2\pi(\mathbf{a}_{1}\times\mathbf{a}_{2})}{\mathbf{a}_{1}\cdot(\mathbf{a}_{2}\times\mathbf{a}_{3})}=(0.85485514\,\textnormal{\AA}^{-1})\ \hat{\mathbf{z}}. $$

In this setup, when no initial magnetic moments are specified, the self-consistent cycle converges to a nonmagnetic, time-reversal- ( $\mathcal{T}$ -) invariant solution (i.e. a state in which the spin density vanishes at all positions in real space). Core electrons were treated by norm-conserving, optimized nonlocal pseudopotentials. The self-consistent calculations were performed over a mesh of $10\times 10\times 5$ ${\bf k}$ points. The kinetic energy cutoff was set to 680 eV. To properly localize the half-filled Eu $4f$ orbitals in the PM state, correct self-interaction errors, and to improve the overall accuracy of the PM-state band structure, a Hubbard $U$ correction of $U=5$ eV on the Eu sites was implemented within the GGA $+$ $U$ scheme [Dudarev1998Electron-energy-lossStudy].

### III.2 Surface spectral function calculation details

We will next use the Wannier-based tight-binding Hamiltonian for the PM phase of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ previously obtained from DFT calculations in Sec. III.1 to compute the $(001)$ -surface states. We begin by cutting the Wannier model into a slab geometry that is finite in the $z$ -direction while retaining periodicity in the $(x,y)$ -plane, resulting in a slab Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{slab}}$ . We then partially Fourier transform $H_{\mathrm{slab}}$ to obtain the slab Bloch Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{slab}}(\mathbf{k})$ , where $\mathbf{k}$ denotes a vector in the space of the in-plane crystal momenta:

$$ \mathbf{k}\equiv(k_{1},k_{2}), $$

where $k_{1,2}$ respectively lie along the reciprocal lattice vectors $\mathbf{b}_{1,2}$ in Eq. (2). The slab Bloch Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{slab}}(\mathbf{k})$ is consequently a square matrix of dimension:

$$ N=N_{s}\times N_{a}\times N_{L}, $$

where $N_{s}=2$ is the number of spin components, $N_{a}=20$ is the number of (Kramers pairs of) orbitals per layer (slab unit cell), and $N_{L}$ is the number of layers. Throughout all of the slab-based calculations in this work, we fix $N_{L}=40$ .

We next define the retarded Green’s function at a given energy $E$ and in-plane momentum $\mathbf{k}$ to be:

$$ G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)=\bigl((E-E_{F})\mathbb{I}_{N\times N}-H_{\mathrm{slab}}(\mathbf{k})+i\Omega\mathbb{I}_{N\times N}\bigr)^{-1}, $$

where $\mathbb{I}_{N\times N}$ is the $N\times N$ identity matrix and $\Omega$ is a phenomenological broadening parameter. For all of the theoretical spectral function calculations in this work, we choose $\Omega=3.87$ meV such that $\Omega$ is equal to $k_{B}T$ for $T=45$ K, which lies just above the temperature range in which our PM-state ARPES measurements were performed (see for example Sec. II). To restrict consideration to spectral weight on the top slab surface, we then construct the top-surface projector:

$$ P_{t}=\sum_{s=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{a=1}^{N_{a}}|\psi_{s,a,N_{L}}\rangle\langle\psi_{s,a,N_{L}}|, $$

where $|\psi_{s,a,i}\rangle$ is a tight-binding (Wannier) basis state of the slab model with a spin index $s$ , an orbital index $a$ , and a layer (slab unit cell) index $i$ (see the text surrounding Eq. (5)). In Eq. (7), $P_{t}$ is hence an $N\times N$ matrix. In the basis of the underlying spins, orbitals, and layers, $P_{t}$ is a diagonal matrix whose elements are equal to $1$ for basis states belonging to the top layer, and are $0$ for all other basis states. Lastly, we define the top-surface spectral function $A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},E)$ at each $\mathbf{k}$ and $E$ by taking the imaginary part of the trace of $G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)$ in Eq. (6) projected to the top surface [Wu2018WannierTools:Materials, Saito2016Tight-bindingFilms]:

$$ A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},E)=-\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[P_{t}G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)P_{t}\bigr]=-\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[P_{t}G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)\bigr], $$

in which we have simplified using the projector idempotence $P_{t}^{2}=P_{t}$ and the cyclic property of the trace.

To make contact between $A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},E)$ and the full density of states, we first examine the full spectral function $A(\mathbf{k},E)$ realized by neglecting (setting to identity) the factor of $P_{t}$ in Eq. (8). We begin this analysis by considering the action of $G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)$ on a Bloch eigenstate $|n\mathbf{k}\rangle$ , for which:

$$ H_{\mathrm{slab}}(\mathbf{k})|n\mathbf{k}\rangle=E_{n}(\mathbf{k})|n\mathbf{k}\rangle. $$

Because $[H_{\mathrm{slab}}(\mathbf{k}),G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)]=0$ , then Eqs. (6) and (9) imply that:

$$ G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)|n\mathbf{k}\rangle=\left(\frac{1}{(E-E_{F})-E_{n}(\mathbf{k})+i\Omega}\right)|n\mathbf{k}\rangle, $$

such that $G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)$ can be re-expressed through the spectral decomposition:

$$ G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{|n\mathbf{k}\rangle\langle n\mathbf{k}|}{(E-E_{F})-E_{n}(\mathbf{k})+i\Omega}. $$

Inserting Eq. (11) into Eq. (8) with $P_{t}$ set to the identity then returns a spectral function $A(\mathbf{k},E)$ for the entire slab at each $\mathbf{k}$ :

$$ \displaystyle A(\mathbf{k},E) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)\bigr] \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,\frac{1}{(E-E_{F})-E_{n}(\mathbf{k})+i\Omega} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\Omega}{[E-E_{F}-E_{n}(\mathbf{k})]^{2}+\Omega^{2}} \displaystyle\equiv \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\delta_{\Omega}\bigl(E-E_{F}-E_{n}(\mathbf{k})\bigr), $$

where in the final line, we recognize the preceding expression as the Lorentzian representation of the Dirac delta function $\delta_{\Omega}(E-E_{F}-E_{n}(\mathbf{k}))$ . The overall spectral function $A(\mathbf{k},E)$ in Eq. (12) hence characterizes the Fourier-transformed density of states [Saito2016Tight-bindingFilms, Fang2013TheoryInsulators, Mahan1990Many-ParticlePhysics]. Due to the strongly nonlinear (delta-function-like) profile of $A(\mathbf{k},E)$ in Eq. (12), we therefore throughout this work plot all spectral functions on a logarithmic scale with arbitrary units (a.u.).

Next, to understand the role of $P_{t}$ in Eq. (8), we simplify the trace in Eq. (8) by combining Eqs. (7) and (11):

$$ \mathrm{Tr}\bigl[P_{t}G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)\bigr]=\sum_{n}\frac{\langle n\mathbf{k}|P_{t}|n\mathbf{k}\rangle}{(E-E_{F})-E_{n}(\mathbf{k})+i\Omega}=\sum_{s=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{a=1}^{N_{a}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\left|\langle\psi_{s,a,N_{L}}|n\mathbf{k}\rangle\right|^{2}}{(E-E_{F})-E_{n}(\mathbf{k})+i\Omega}. $$

Because each overlap magnitude $|\langle\psi_{s,a,N_{L}}|n\mathbf{k}\rangle|^{2}$ in Eq. (13) is real, then using Eq. (12), the surface spectral function $A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},E)$ in Eq. (8) becomes:

$$ \displaystyle A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},E) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{s=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{a=1}^{N_{a}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left|\langle\psi_{s,a,N_{L}}|n\mathbf{k}\rangle\right|^{2}\left[-\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,\frac{1}{(E-E_{F})-E_{n}(\mathbf{k})+i\Omega}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{s=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{a=1}^{N_{a}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left|\langle\psi_{s,a,N_{L}}|n\mathbf{k}\rangle\right|^{2}\delta_{\Omega}\bigl(E-E_{F}-E_{n}(\mathbf{k})\bigr). $$

Overall, the form of Eq. (14) indicates that $A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},E)$ is similar in structure to the total spectral function $A(\mathbf{k},E)$ in Eq. (12), but instead measures the weight of each slab Bloch eigenstate $|n\mathbf{k}\rangle$ at $E-E_{F}$ on the top surface via the combination of $\delta_{\Omega}(E-E_{F}-E_{n}(\mathbf{k}))$ and the overlap magnitudes of $|n\mathbf{k}\rangle$ with the top-surface basis states. In Fig. S3b, we show the $(001)$ -surface spectral function of the PM state of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ computed using Eq. (8). The surface spectrum consists of a single hyperbolic feature that lies within the continuum of unoccupied bulk states (the projected bulk conduction manifold).

Before analyzing the angular momentum textures and topological origin of the unoccupied $(001)$ -surface states in Fig. S3b (which will shortly be done in Secs. III.3 and III.4), we will establish the degree to which the chemical potential of the surface states $\widetilde{E}=E_{F}+$0.34\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ depends on our bulk calculation details. This information is especially important because the unoccupied surface states in our ARPES measurements appear at relatively higher energies, specifically instead exhibiting a band minimum at $E_{0}\approx E_{F}+$0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ as estimated from the kinetic energy of photoelectrons. First, $\widetilde{E}$ depends on the choice of surface termination atoms in our slab model, an effect that itself is typically significant in models of the surface states of real solid-state materials [Shockley1939OnPotential, Lee2023Layer-by-layerStates, Wu2020DistinctMnBi4Te7]. Furthermore, in our $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ samples, we do not have atomistic knowledge of the $(001)$ -surface probed in our ARPES experiments with which to calibrate the slab surface termination in our DFT- and Wannier-based surface-state calculations. Next, $\widetilde{E}$ in Fig. S3b is also dependent on the value of $U$ employed in our bulk DFT $+$ SOC $+$ $U$ calculations (Sec. III.1). Specifically, in modeling the PM state of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ , we have incorporated a large Coulomb term $U=5$ eV in our DFT $+$ SOC $+$ $U$ calculations to shift the half-filled, nearly-flat Eu 4 $f$ states away from $E_{F}$ . The choice of $U$ in turn influences the surface-state chemical potential $\widetilde{E}$ via the spectral weight of the Eu 4 $f$ orbitals in the surface bands.

We therefore next quantify the contribution of Eu 4 $f$ states to the surface spectrum. To accomplish this, we first construct a projector $P_{4f}$ onto the Eu $4f$ states in the slab model:

$$ P_{4f}=\sum_{s=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{a\in\{\text{Eu}_{4f}\}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{L}}|\psi_{s,a,i}\rangle\langle\psi_{s,a,i}|, $$

where $|\psi_{s,a,i}\rangle$ and $N_{L}$ are defined in the text surrounding Eq. (7). Similar to $P_{t}$ in Eq. (7), when $P_{4f}$ is placed in the basis of the spins, orbitals, and layers of the slab model, $P_{4f}$ is a diagonal matrix whose elements are equal to $1$ for basis states belonging to the Eu $4f$ orbital subspace, and are $0$ for all other basis states. Using Eqs. (6), (7), and (15), we then define a spectral function $\langle\text{Eu}_{4f}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ that is only large for the subset of the surface spectral weight that derives from the Eu $4f$ orbitals:

$$ \langle\text{Eu}_{4f}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle=-\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[P_{4f}P_{t}G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)P_{t}\bigr]. $$

To better understand the properties of the unoccupied surface bands in Fig. S3b, and to draw connection with our circular dichroism (CD-) ARPES experiments (Sec. II), we will next extract the spin and OAM textures of the $(001)$ -surface states. We will then introduce and analyze a simple ${\bf k}\cdot{\bf p}$ model that reproduces the dispersion and angular momentum textures of the surface conduction bands in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ .

First, to compute the spin texture, we introduce the surface-projected, spin-dependent spectral function vector $\langle{\bf S}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ , whose components are given by [Saito2016Tight-bindingFilms, Kohsaka2017Spin-orbitInterference, Chang2017UnconventionalRhSi, Schirmann2025Geometry-EnforcedMetals]:

$$ \langle S_{\alpha}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle=-\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[\hat{S}_{\alpha}\,P_{t}G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)P_{t}\bigr], $$

where $G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)$ and $P_{t}$ are respectively defined in Eqs. (6) and (7), and where $\hat{S}_{\alpha}$ is the $\alpha$ -th component of the spin operator vector $\hat{\bf S}=(\hat{S}_{x},\hat{S}_{y},\hat{S}_{z})$ . In the basis of the spins and orbitals in the slab Wannier model of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ constructed in Secs. III.1 and III.2, and in reduced units in which the spin eigenvalues are $\pm 1$ , the spin operator components $\hat{S}_{\alpha}$ are represented as $N_{a}N_{L}N_{s}\times N_{a}N_{L}N_{s}=N\times N$ matrices $S_{\alpha}$ :

$$ S_{\alpha}=\mathbb{I}_{N_{a}N_{L}\times N_{a}N_{L}}\,\sigma_{\alpha},\qquad\alpha=x,y,z, $$

where $\sigma_{x,y,z}$ are $2\times 2$ Pauli matrices that act in the spin subspace, $\mathbb{I}_{N_{a}N_{L}\times N_{a}N_{L}}$ is the $N_{a}N_{L}\times N_{a}N_{L}$ identity matrix, and where $N_{a}=20$ and $N_{L}=40$ are respectively the number of Kramers pairs of orbitals in each unit cell of the bulk Wannier model and the number of layers in the slab Hamiltonian (Eq. (5)). In order to ensure that the representation $S_{\alpha}$ of $\hat{S}_{\alpha}$ is ${\bf k}$ -independent in the tight-binding (periodic) gauge of $H_{\mathrm{slab}}(\mathbf{k})$ (Eq. (9)) in which physical and topological quantities are correctly embedded [Yu2011EquivalentConnection, Benalcazar2017ElectricInsulators, Lin2024Spin-resolvedInsulators], we have constructed the Wannier model in a manner in which the up- and down-spin components of each Wannier orbital in Table S1 occupy the same positions in real space. Because $\langle{\bf S}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ is odd under $\mathcal{T}$ and even under $\mathcal{I}$ (i.e. transforms as a $\mathcal{T}$ -odd axial vector), $\langle{\bf S}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ must vanish in bulk systems with $\mathcal{I}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ symmetry. However, on the 2D surfaces of 3D systems, which cannot carry $\mathcal{I}$ as a symmetry [Wieder2016Spin-orbitGroups], $\langle{\bf S}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ can be nonvanishing. Like the surface spectral function $A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},E)$ in Eq. (8), we throughout this work plot $\langle S_{\alpha}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ on a log scale with arbitrary units (a.u.), but now allow for signed data represented using a color map in which blue is positive and red is negative.

To provide context for the spin texture, we first in Fig. S6a plot a constant-energy cut of the total $(001)$ -surface spectral function $A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},E)$ (Eq. (8)) taken $0.23$ eV above the surface-state minimum $\widetilde{E}$ (the dashed line in Figs. S3b and S4a), which approximately corresponds to the same energy offset from the experimental surface-state band minimum $E_{0}$ as our constant-energy ARPES measurements (see Sec. II and the text following Eq. (16)). The total surface spectral function in Fig. S6a is dominated by a nearly circular feature surrounding ${\bf k}={\bf 0}$ with weaker hexagonal corrections. We then in Fig. S6b plot the $\langle S_{xz}\rangle=\langle\frac{S_{x}+S_{z}}{\sqrt{2}}\rangle$ component of the spin-dependent spectral function $\langle{\bf S}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ (Eq. (17)) at the same constant energy as $A_{\mathrm{surf}}(\mathbf{k},E)$ in Fig. S6a, where we have selected the $\langle S_{xz}\rangle$ component to match the alignment of our experimental CD-ARPES probe of the OAM texture (further detailed below in the text following Eq. (38)). Surprisingly, $\langle S_{xz}({\bf k},E)\rangle$ in Fig. S6b consists of two concentric rings with alternatingly signed $\langle S_{xz}\rangle$ spin polarizations. This indicates that the circular surface spectral feature in Fig. S6a is in fact not one surface Fermi pocket, but is rather two narrowly split Fermi pockets that together originate from a 2D surface Dirac cone with extremely weak SOC splitting. As we will discuss below in Sec. III.4, the $(001)$ -surface Dirac cone at ${\bf k}={\bf 0}$ in our Wannier-based calculations of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ can more specifically be viewed as the 2D topological surface state of a 3D topological band insulator phase [Hasan2010Colloquium:Insulators, Wieder2022TopologicalSymmetry] at an electronic filling above the Fermi level $\nu>\nu_{F}$ (Eq. (3)), which can be accessed by photo-doping experiments like those in the present study.

We next turn our attention to the orbital texture of the $(001)$ -surface states, which is closely linked to our CD-ARPES experiments. Specifically, of the different ${\bf k}$ -resolved contributions to the orbital magnetization, CD-ARPES most directly couples to the local (in real space) contribution to the OAM from the underlying atomic orbitals [Park2011Orbital-angular-momentumSplitting, Park2012ChiralBi2Se3, Wang2013CircularInsulators, Yen2024ControllableSemimetals]. To probe the atomic-orbital contribution to the OAM, we construct a surface-projected, OAM-dependent spectral function vector $\langle{\bf L}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ , analogous to the surface-projected, spin-dependent spectral function vector $\langle{\bf S}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ in Eq. (17), whose components are given by [Sidilkover2025ReexaminingInsulator, Schirmann2025Geometry-EnforcedMetals]:

$$ \langle L_{\alpha}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle=-\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,\mathrm{Tr}\bigl[\hat{L}_{\alpha}\,P_{t}G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)P_{t}\bigr], $$

where $G^{R}(\mathbf{k},E)$ and $P_{t}$ are respectively defined in Eqs. (6) and (7), and where $\hat{L}_{\alpha}$ is the $\alpha$ -th component of the OAM operator vector $\hat{\bf L}=(\hat{L}_{x},\hat{L}_{y},\hat{L}_{z})$ . Like $\langle{\bf S}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ in Eq. (17), $\langle{\bf L}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ transforms as a $\mathcal{T}$ -odd axial vector, and must hence vanish at each ${\bf k}$ in bulk systems with $\mathcal{I}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ symmetry. However, on the 2D surfaces of 3D systems, $\langle{\bf L}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ can similarly be nonvanishing due to the absence of 3D $\mathcal{I}$ (specifically $\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{T}$ ) symmetry.

Unlike the spin operator components $\hat{S}_{\alpha}$ , the OAM operator components $\hat{L}_{\alpha}$ have more complicated representations in the Wannier basis, and are also more sensitive to the numerical Wannierization procedure. Specifically, in order to interpret $\langle L_{\alpha}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ as a physical observable, it is crucial that the value of $\langle L_{\alpha}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ at each ${\bf k}$ does not depend on the arbitrary piece of the gauge of the wavefunctions $|n\mathbf{k}\rangle$ (Eq. (9)) of the slab Bloch Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{slab}}(\mathbf{k})$ (i.e. the free gauge factors that do not affect the real-space model embedding [Yu2011EquivalentConnection, Benalcazar2017ElectricInsulators, Lin2024Spin-resolvedInsulators]). This can most straightforwardly be accomplished by requiring that, like $S_{\alpha}$ in Eq. (18), each OAM operator component $\hat{L}_{\alpha}$ is represented as a ${\bf k}$ -independent matrix $L_{\alpha}$ in the tight-binding (periodic) gauge of $H_{\mathrm{slab}}(\mathbf{k})$ . In turn, in order for the matrix representatives $L_{\alpha}$ of $\hat{L}_{\alpha}$ to be ${\bf k}$ -independent, each of the Wannier orbitals associated to the same atomic shell of each atom – specifically the Wannier orbitals for each atom that are assigned the same principal ( $n$ ) and azimuthal ( $\ell$ , i.e. OAM) quantum numbers – must occupy the same positions in real space. This ensures that each OAM operator component $\hat{L}_{\alpha}$ acts locally on the real-space tight-binding basis states, such that the basis-state positions remain invariant under the action of $\hat{L}_{\alpha}$ for all $\alpha$ . In the Wannier tight-binding model that we constructed for the PM state of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ in Sec. III.1, the basis-state positions (Table S1) not only satisfy the above requirement, but are even more tightly grouped. Specifically, as shown in Table S1, each of the Wannier orbitals in our model coincides with the position of its associated atom to within $10^{-4}$ in the units of the lattice vectors $\mathbf{a}_{1,2,3}$ in Eq. (1). Our Wannier model is hence suitably constructed for computing the surface-state OAM texture $\langle{\bf L}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ in Eq. (19).

Having established that the surface OAM texture $\langle{\bf L}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ can be computed by applying Eq. (19) to our Wannier tight-binding model, we next turn our attention to constructing the OAM matrix representatives $L_{\alpha}$ in the Wannier basis. In reduced units in which $\hbar=1$ , the OAM operator components $\hat{L}_{\alpha}$ are specifically represented in the slab Wannier model constructed in Sec. III.2 as $N_{a}N_{L}N_{s}\times N_{a}N_{L}N_{s}=N\times N$ matrices $L_{\alpha}$ that each take a block form:

$$ L_{\alpha}=\left\{\bigoplus_{\xi,\ell_{\xi}\neq 0}L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\alpha}\right\}\oplus\left\{\bigoplus_{\xi,\ell_{\xi}=0}\mathbb{0}_{N_{s}N_{L}\times N_{s}N_{L}}\right\}, $$

where each $L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\alpha}$ is proportional to the identity in the $N_{s}N_{L}\times N_{s}N_{L}=2N_{L}\times 2N_{L}$ spin and layer subspace (Eq. (5)), and where $\mathbb{0}_{N_{s}N_{L}\times N_{s}N_{L}}$ is the $N_{s}N_{L}\times N_{s}N_{L}$ matrix of zeroes. In Eq. (20), $\xi$ and $\ell_{\xi}$ respectively run in Table S1 over the “Site” column and the OAM quantum numbers $\ell_{\xi}$ per site in the “Wannier Orbitals” column, such that for example the $\ell=2$ $d$ and $\ell=3$ $f$ orbitals of the $1a$ Eu atom are included in the first direct sum ( $\ell_{\xi}\neq 0$ ) and excluded in the second ( $\ell_{\xi}=0$ ), whereas for example the $\ell=0$ $s$ orbitals of the $2d$ Cd atoms are excluded from the first direct sum and included in the second. Each $L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\alpha}$ in Eq. (20) is hence an $N_{L}N_{s}(2\ell_{\xi}+1)\times N_{L}N_{s}(2\ell_{\xi}+1)$ matrix [Griffiths2016IntroductionMechanics].

To obtain the matrices $L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\alpha}$ in Eq. (20) in the Wannier tight-binding basis, we first recognize that each atomic orbital in our model is expressed in the real cubic–harmonic basis [Muggli1972CubicHarmonics]:

$$ \bigl\{s,p_{x},p_{y},p_{z},d_{z^{2}},d_{xz},d_{yz},d_{x^{2}-y^{2}},d_{xy},\ldots\bigr\}, $$

rather than in the complex spherical–harmonic basis $\{\,Y_{\ell}^{m}\,\}$ in which $L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{z}$ is a diagonal matrix whose only nonzero elements take values given by the orbital magnetic quantum numbers $m$ [Griffiths2016IntroductionMechanics, McQuarrie1997PhysicalApproach]. Our strategy for constructing each $L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{x,y,z}$ matrix therefore consists of two steps: we first construct $L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{x,y,z}$ in the familiar basis of spherical harmonics, and we then apply a unitary transformation to rotate $L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{x,y,z}$ into the cubic-harmonic Wannier basis.

We next recognize that given an OAM matrix representative $(L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{z})^{(\ell)}$ in the spherical-harmonic basis (denoted by the superscript $(\ell)$ here and below) with the eigenstates $|\ell,m\rangle$ such that:

$$ (L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{z})^{(\ell)}|\ell,m\rangle=m|\ell,m\rangle, $$

there exist ladder operators $\hat{L}_{\pm}^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}$ that change $m$ by one unit within the $\ell_{\xi}$ manifold [Sakurai2017ModernMechanics]:

$$ \hat{L}^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\pm}\,|\ell,m\rangle=\sqrt{\ell_{\xi}(\ell_{\xi}+1)-m(m\pm 1)}\;|\ell,m\pm 1\rangle. $$

Using Eq. (23), we then construct the matrix representatives $(L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\pm})^{(\ell)}$ of $\hat{L}^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\pm}$ , whose matrix elements are given by:

$$ \left[(L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\pm})^{(\ell)}\right]_{m,m^{\prime}}=\sqrt{\ell_{\xi}(\ell_{\xi}+1)-m^{\prime}(m^{\prime}\pm 1)}\;\delta_{m,m^{\prime}\pm 1}. $$

The $\alpha=x,y,z$ OAM matrix representatives in the spherical-harmonic basis are then by definition given by [Sakurai2017ModernMechanics, Griffiths2016IntroductionMechanics]:

$$ (L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{x})^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{2}\left\{(L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{+})^{(\ell)}+(L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{-})^{(\ell)}\right\},\qquad(L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{y})^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{2i}\left\{(L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{+})^{(\ell)}-(L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{-})^{(\ell)}\right\}. $$

Lastly, each cubic-harmonic (Wannier-basis) eigenstate $|\ell,\mu\rangle_{\rm cub}$ represents a linear combination of the spherical-harmonic eigenstates $|\ell,m\rangle$ [Muggli1972CubicHarmonics]:

$$ |\ell,\mu\rangle_{\rm cub}=\sum_{m=-\ell}^{+\ell}\left[U^{\ell}\right]_{\mu m}\,|\ell,m\rangle. $$

Using Eq. (26), we hence obtain the unitary matrix $U^{\ell}$ that transforms the OAM matrix representatives $(L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\alpha})^{(\ell)}$ in the spherical-harmonic basis into the OAM matrix representatives $L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\alpha}$ in the cubic-harmonic basis of our Wannier tight-binding model (Eq. (20)):

$$ L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\alpha}=U^{\ell}\,(L^{\xi,\ell_{\xi}}_{\alpha})^{(\ell)}\,\big(U^{\ell}\big)^{\dagger},\qquad\alpha\in\{x,y,z\}. $$

As shown in Table S1, our Wannier model contains $s$ ( $\ell=0$ ), $p$ ( $\ell=1$ ), $d$ ( $\ell=2$ ), and $f$ ( $\ell=3$ ) orbitals. Using the procedure detailed in Eqs. (20) through (27), we may now construct the OAM matrix representatives $L_{\alpha}$ required to compute $\langle{\bf L}(\mathbf{k},E)\rangle$ in Eq. (19). For each of the orbital shells with $\ell\neq 0$ enumerated below, we will specifically provide explicit matrix representatives in the form of $(2\ell+1)\times(2\ell+1)$ square matrices, each of which is taken to be shorthand notation for a larger $N_{L}N_{s}(2\ell+1)\times N_{L}N_{s}(2\ell+1)$ matrix that is proportional to the identity in the $N_{s}N_{L}\times N_{s}N_{L}$ spin and layer subspace (Eq. (5)).

First, for the $p$ shell of the $2d$ As atoms (denoted with $\xi,\ell_{\xi}\equiv(p)$ ), the real cubic harmonics are expressed in terms of the spherical harmonics $Y_{1}^{m}$ as:

$$ p_{z}=Y_{1}^{0},\qquad p_{x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(Y_{1}^{-1}-Y_{1}^{1}\bigr),\qquad p_{y}=\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(Y_{1}^{-1}+Y_{1}^{1}\bigr). $$

In the cubic-harmonic ordering $\{p_{z},p_{x},p_{y}\}$ , the ladder operators $L^{(p)}_{\pm}$ in the Wannier basis are then represented by:

$$ L^{(p)}_{+}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&-i\\
-1&0&0\\
i&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad L^{(p)}_{-}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&-i\\
1&0&0\\
i&0&0\end{pmatrix}, $$

and the block $3\times 3$ OAM representatives $L_{\alpha}^{(p)}$ , $\alpha\in\{x,y,z\}$ in the Wannier basis are given by:

$$ L_{x}^{(p)}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&-i\\
0&0&0\\
i&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad L_{y}^{(p)}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i&0\\
i&0&0\\
0&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad L_{z}^{(p)}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\
0&0&i\\
0&-i&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

Next, for the $d$ shell of the $1a$ Eu atom (denoted with $\xi,\ell_{\xi}\equiv(d)$ ), the real cubic harmonics are expressed in terms of the spherical harmonics $Y_{2}^{m}$ as:

### III.4 Topological classification and band topology above the Fermi level in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$

In our calculations of the $(001)$ -surface spectrum of the PM phase of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ in Secs. III.2 and III.3, we observed (weakly SOC-split) 2D surface Dirac bands around ${\bf k}={\bf 0}$ with an energy minimum $\widetilde{E}$ above the Fermi level $E_{F}$ (Figs. S3b, S5a, and S6). We will next investigate whether it is possible to associate the unoccupied Dirac surface states in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ to bulk topological bands.

To address this question, we employ the approach of Ref. [Vergniory2022AllMaterials], in which the methods of Topological Quantum Chemistry [Bradlyn2017TopologicalChemistry, Elcoro2021MagneticChemistry, Wieder2022TopologicalSymmetry] and symmetry-based indicators (SIs) [Kruthoff2017TopologicalCombinatorics, PoHoiChun2017Symmetry-basedGroups, SongZhida2018QuantitativeSolids, Khalaf2018SymmetryInsulators] were applied to efficiently screen band structures in nonmagnetic materials (or material phases) at and away from $E_{F}$ for nontrivial topology that is detectable from crystal symmetry eigenvalues. The authors of Ref. [Vergniory2022AllMaterials] specifically first performed DFT calculations using the Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package (VASP) [Kresse1996EfficiencySet, Kresse1996EfficientSet], then applied the freely accessible Fortran program VASP2Trace (https://github.com/zjwang11/irvsp) [Gao2021Irvsp:VASP] to extract the eigenvalues of the unitary crystal symmetries, and lastly uploaded the extracted symmetry eigenvalues to the Check Topological Mat tool on the Bilbao Crystallographic Server (BCS) to determine the band topology (accessible by navigating from http://webbdcrista2.ehu.es/ to https://cryst.ehu.es/cgi-bin/cryst/programs/magnetictopo.pl?tipog=gesp) [Aroyo2006BilbaoPrograms, Aroyo2006BilbaoGroups, Aroyo2011CrystallographyServer, Vergniory2019AMaterials]. Because our DFT calculations in Sec. III.1 were performed using Quantum Espresso [Giannozzi2009QUANTUMMaterials, Giannozzi2017AdvancedESPRESSO, Giannozzi2020QuantumExascale] and not VASP, we began by implementing custom code, detailed below, to extract the crystal symmetry eigenvalues from our band structure calculations in a format compatible with Check Topological Mat.

To construct an input file for Check Topological Mat from our DFT band structure calculation in Fig. S3a, we first analyzed nonmagnetic SG 164 ( $P\bar{3}m1$ ), the 3D symmetry group $G$ of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ in the PM state, to determine the set of maximal ${\bf k}$ points (i.e. the $\mathcal{T}$ -invariant ${\bf k}$ points, as well as high-symmetry points without $\mathcal{T}$ like $K$ and $H$ in Fig. S3a, see Refs. [Bradlyn2017TopologicalChemistry, Elcoro2021MagneticChemistry]). At each maximal ${\bf k}$ point, there specifically exists an infinite subgroup of symmetries $G_{\bf k}\subseteq G$ , termed the little group, for which each symmetry:

$$ g\in G_{\bf k}, $$

leaves ${\bf k}$ invariant up to an integer linear combination ${\bf K}$ of the reciprocal lattice vectors $\mathbf{b}_{1,2,3}$ in Eq. (2):

$$ g{\bf k}\text{ mod }{\bf K}={\bf k}. $$

For each grouping of bands that share the same energy eigenvalue $E_{n\mathbf{k}}$ (up to a numerical tolerance factor of $0.002$ eV), we next obtained the set of $m$ (approximately) degenerate Bloch eigenstates $\{|\psi^{1}_{n\mathbf{k}}\rangle,|\psi^{2}_{n\mathbf{k}}\rangle,\ldots,|\psi^{m}_{n\mathbf{k}}\rangle\}$ in an orthonormal basis. The $m$ states that share the energy $E_{n\mathbf{k}}$ may either form an enforced degeneracy, or may simply be a set of states for which SOC and orbital splitting is very weak, but in either case transform into themselves or other degenerate states in the set under the action of the little group symmetries $g\in G_{\bf k}$ [Bradley1972TheSolids, Bradlyn2017TopologicalChemistry].

Using the spglib software library [Togo2024Spglib:Search], we then obtained a finite set of coset symmetry representatives with respect to the infinite group of translations for the full SG $G$ , and restricted consideration to those that are also coset representatives of $G_{\bf k}$ using Eq. (45). Of the coset representatives of $G_{\bf k}$ obtained from spglib, a smaller subset consists only of unitary symmetries $O$ , which hence carry eigenvalues that can be numerically obtained. Specifically, each unitary coset representative $O\in G_{\bf k}$ admits a decomposition of the form [Seitz1936TheCrystals, Bradley1972TheSolids]:

$$ O=\{R|t\}, $$

where $R$ is a point group operation and $t$ is a (possibly fractional) translation. For the $m$ (approximately) degenerate Bloch states with energy $E_{n\mathbf{k}}$ , the action of the unitary little group symmetry $O$ is represented by an $m\times m$ matrix $O^{\mathbf{k}}$ :

$$ O|\psi^{i}_{n\mathbf{k}}\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left[O^{\mathbf{k}}\right]_{ij}\,|\psi^{j}_{n\mathbf{k}}\rangle, $$

where the matrix elements of $O^{\mathbf{k}}$ are hence given by:

$$ \left[O^{\mathbf{k}}\right]_{ij}=\langle\psi^{j}_{n\mathbf{k}}|\,O\,|\psi^{i}_{n\mathbf{k}}\rangle. $$

In the plane-wave spinor basis of our DFT calculations, $O$ in Eq. (46) acts by transforming $\mathbf{k}$ vectors under $R$ , multiplying by the phase factor $e^{-i(R\mathbf{k})\cdot t}$ from the combined action of $R$ and $t$ , and by applying the SU(2) spin rotation that corresponds to the proper rotation piece of $R$ . For each $O$ and (approximate) band multiplet at $E_{n\mathbf{k}}$ , we lastly obtain a character (trace) $\chi_{n\mathbf{k}}(O)$ by computing:

$$ \chi_{n\mathbf{k}}(O)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\langle\psi^{i}_{n\mathbf{k}}|O|\psi^{i}_{n\mathbf{k}}\rangle=\mathrm{Tr}\ O^{\mathbf{k}}. $$

The characters $\chi_{n\mathbf{k}}(O)$ are equal to the sum of the symmetry eigenvalues of $O$ for the $m$ degenerate states at $E_{n\mathbf{k}}$ , and across all maximal ${\bf k}$ points and band degeneracies form a set of symmetry data vectors that can be used to determine band connectivity and topology [Bradlyn2017TopologicalChemistry, Elcoro2021MagneticChemistry].
