$$ \nu_{F}=51. $$

Owing to the requirement from $\mathcal{T}$ symmetry that noninteracting, nonmagnetic insulators have even numbers of occupied bands [Watanabe2015FillingCrystals, Wieder2016Spin-orbitGroups], $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ in the PM state is therefore, in the language of Ref. [Vergniory2022AllMaterials], an enforced semimetal with a Fermi degeneracy (ESFD) at $\nu=\nu_{F}$ , and not a band insulator. The first gap in the PM state of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ allowed by symmetry instead occurs at a filling of $\nu=\nu_{F}+1=52$ electrons, as indicated by the dashed horizontal line in Table S2. Remarkably, not only does the gap at $\nu=52$ in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ carry the cumulative topology of a 3D TI state ( $Z_{4}=3$ in “all type / top. ind.”), but in fact all of the symmetry-allowed band gaps realize 3D TI states over a range of $\Delta\nu=12$ electrons spanning from $\nu=\nu_{F}-5=46$ to $\nu=\nu_{F}+7=58$ . Hence, though surface chemical potentials may still shift topological surface Dirac cones away from the average energy of nontrivial band-insulating gaps (see the text following Eq. (14)), the huge filling range $\Delta\nu=12$ of nontrivial 3D TI gaps surrounding $\nu_{F}$ in Table S2 is much larger than the scale of chemical potential effects, implying that the unoccupied $(001)$ -surface Dirac cone in our DFT calculations (Figs. S3b, S5a, and S6) can be associated to a band-insulating 3D TI phase with $\nu\neq\nu_{F}$ . Even further restricting to fillings above the Fermi energy $\nu>\nu_{F}$ , it is also unlikely that surface chemical potential effects can shift a Dirac cone by energies equivalent to changing $\nu$ by $7$ electrons, and we may hence more specifically reasonably associate the $(001)$ -surface Dirac cone in Figs. S3b, S5a, and S6 to the smaller set of unoccupied 3D TI gaps with $\nu_{F}<\nu\leq 58$ in Table S2.

In this sense, $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ is reminiscent of the repeat-topological (RTopo) materials introduced in Ref. [Vergniory2022AllMaterials], especially the example of Bi2Mg3, which respects the same symmetry group SG 164 ( $P\bar{3}m1$ ) as $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ in the PM state. RTopo materials were specifically defined in Ref. [Vergniory2022AllMaterials] as materials that are stable topological band insulators at intrinsic filling $\nu_{F}$ , but also host cumulative stable topological band-insulating states at the first band gap below $\nu_{F}$ allowed by symmetry. In Bi2Mg3, the RTopo classification gives rise to two sets of $(001)$ -surface topological Dirac cones, which at intrinsic filling respectively manifest as surface states in the projected gap just above $E_{F}$ , and as surface resonance bands below $E_{F}$ that coexist with the surface projections of the bulk valence manifold and are associated to the topological band gap at $\nu<\nu_{F}$ [Vergniory2022AllMaterials, Chang2019RealizationMg3Bi2, Zhou2019ExperimentalEpitaxy]. S3b, S5a, and S6) and the associated topological band gaps at $\nu>\nu_{F}$ in Table S2 can hence be viewed as a generalization of the concept of repeat-topology – originally introduced to predict topological boundary states accessible in equilibrium ARPES experiments at intrinsic filling – to topological surface conduction bands that are accessible by doping and pump-probe ARPES experiments like those in the present study.

In this section, we use electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) measurements to confirm the energy above the Fermi level $E_{F}$ of the bulk conduction band that is nondispersing to leading order at ${\bf k}={\bf 0}$ (the bulk $\Gamma$ point, see Fig. S3a). First, in Fig. 4b of the main text, we plot our EELS measurements at low energies, which show a strong peak at approximately $0.12\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ that we attribute to a plasmon. Here, in Fig. S9a, we plot EELS measurements at higher energies taken on the $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ samples used in this study. The higher-energy EELS measurements in Fig. S9a show a broad continuum of energy loss above $E-E_{F}\approx$0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ , indicative of either a bulk or surface band minimum at that energy. Consistent with this observation, our first-principles electronic band structure calculations in Sec. III also show a weakly dispersing bulk conduction band at $\Gamma$ with approximately the same energy $E_{CBM}$ (Fig. S3a). Furthermore, the value of $E_{CBM}\approx E_{F}+$0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ obtained from our EELS measurements is also in agreement with previous optical spectroscopy measurements on samples characterized as semimetallic [Wu2024TheSingularity], which place a conduction band minimum between $0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ and $0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ relative to the maximum of the hole-like valence band. Optical spectroscopy and Tr-ARPES studies of semiconducting samples [Santos-Cottin2023EuCd2As2:Semiconductor] similarly place a local conduction band minimum at $0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ .

Next, we additionally analyze our Tr-ARPES data to confirm the position of this bulk conduction band relative to $E_{0}$ , the minimum of the unoccupied surface states. Returning to the analysis of our ARPES data at low fluence excitation, in a one-band quasi-equilibrium system, the ARPES intensity can be written as [Boschini2024Time-resolvedMaterials, Damascelli2003Angle-resolvedSuperconductors]:

$$ I(k,E)=A(k,E)|M(k,E)|^{2}f(E), $$

where $f(E)$ is the Fermi-Dirac distribution, $M(k,E)$ is a matrix element for the excitation of a bound electron to a plane-wave state, and $A(k,E)$ is the single-particle spectral function, given by:

$$ A(k,E)=-\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\Sigma^{\prime\prime}(k,E)}{\left[E-\epsilon(k)-\Sigma^{\prime}(k,E)\right]^{2}+\left[\Sigma^{\prime\prime}(k,E)\right]^{2}}. $$

In Eq. (53), $\epsilon(k)$ is a single-particle energy eigenvalue, and $\Sigma^{\prime}(k,E)=\text{Re }\Sigma$ and $\Sigma^{\prime\prime}(k,E)=\text{Im }\Sigma$ are respectively the real and imaginary parts of the self energy, which are connected through the Kramers-Kronig relations. If we assume $\Sigma^{\prime\prime}$ to be independent of $k$ (that is, scattering mechanisms encoded by $\Sigma^{\prime\prime}$ are assumed to vary slowly with momentum), cuts of $A(k,E)$ taken at constant $E$ have a Lorentzian profile in $k$ centered at $\epsilon(k)+\Sigma^{\prime}(E)$ with a half width at half maximum (HWHM) proportional to $\Sigma^{\prime\prime}$ .

Under the assumption that $\text{Im }\Sigma$ is $k$ -independent, we next use Eq. (53) to track the dispersion and imaginary self energy of the unoccupied surface states via Lorentzian fits of the MDCs measured at low excitation fluence. Our ARPES spectra were prepared by integrating over a short window starting at $t=t_{0}$ to account for rapid intra-band scattering and to allow significant spectral weight at all energy levels. A representative example ARPES spectrum from our data is shown in Fig. S11a. Since we do not observe band renormalization or other time-dependent photovoltage shifts in our ARPES measurements (see Sec. VII and Fig. 3a of the main text), the results of this fitting process are independent of our choice of the integration duration. In Fig. S11b, we show the corresponding waterfall plots from the ARPES data in Fig. S11a. The fits in Fig. S11b show good agreement with individual cuts, although the raw MDCs exhibit some observable asymmetry – particularly at high energies – resulting in small deviations from the fits. Though not shown above, we further find that the deviations from the fits persist if we instead employ a two-Lorentzian model (with the restriction from symmetry that the two peaks of the Lorentzians be at $\pm k_{\text{fit}}$ ). From this, we deduce that the asymmetry in the raw MDCs in Fig. S11b can be attributed to $k$ -dependent terms in the imaginary part of the self energy $\text{Im }\Sigma$ , which we previously neglected for simplicity.

Nevertheless, because our single-Lorentzian fits with $k$ -independent $\text{Im }\Sigma$ exhibit significantly higher numerical stability, carry a reduced number of free parameters, and have a lower reliance on extremely precise initial guess values compared to two-Lorentzian fits or more complicated models with $k$ -dependent $\Sigma$ , we focus our analysis in the main text only on results from single-Lorentzian fits with $k$ -independent $\text{Im }\Sigma$ (Fig. 4a of the main text, the raw spectrum and waterfall plot for which are shown in Fig. S11a,b). In Fig. S11c, we lastly show the $k$ -independent imaginary self energy $\text{Im }\Sigma$ extracted from our single-Lorentzian fits.

In wide-gap semiconductors, it is well established that Tr-ARPES measurements can be affected by photovoltage effects that shift the effective Fermi level probed by ARPES [Schmitt2022FormationTime] and band gap renormalization [Chen2018BandPhosphorus]. If present, these effects could shift the bottom of the surface spectral feature at $E_{0}\approx E_{F}+$0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ (respectively indicated by blue and dark yellow triangles in Fig. S12a,b) upwards to the exciton energy $E_{X}=E_{0}+$100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ (determined below in Fig. S14b and the surrounding text), leading to an apparent long-lived population at the middle of the dispersion extracted at $t\approx$0\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$$ .

To investigate these effects in our measurements, we track in Fig. S12 the position of the local minimum of the ARPES linewidth (indicated by the half width at half maximum, HWHM) as a function of energy under low (Fig. S12a) and high (Fig. S12b) excitation fluence using the fitting process detailed in Sec. VI. We specifically noted in Sec. VI (in particular in the discussion of Fig. S11) that the HWHM of ARPES MDCs are generally proportional to the imaginary self energy $\text{Im }\Sigma(E)$ of the unoccupied states. From this, we then extracted $\text{Im }\Sigma$ under low and intermediate fluence excitation, when the excitonic population can be neglected. Under high fluence excitation, the analogous interpretation of ARPES linewidths is only strictly valid at energies where spectral weight contributed by excitonic populations is negligible, that is, far from the exciton energy, which here lies at $E_{X}=E_{0}+$100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ (Fig. S14b). However, to facilitate a more direct interpretation of our data, and for completeness, we nevertheless plot the ARPES linewidth HWHM at high excitation fluence in Fig. S12b across larger energy ranges that extend to $E_{X}$ .

Overall, the data in Fig. S12 show that the global minimum HWHM appears at approximately $E_{0}$ at all delay times, irrespective of the excitation fluence. We attribute this HWHM minimum to the bottom of the unoccupied surface states, and conclude that the minimum of the surface band does not exhibit time-dependent photovoltage shifts. This allows to us to exclude a particularly significant trivial (non-excitonic) interpretation of our data, as we have shown that the persistent population interpreted in this work as an exciton is not simply an accumulation of electrons at the bottom of a shifted or renormalized unoccupied band.

### VIII.1 Data Processing

We begin in Fig. S13a by plotting a momentum-integrated ARPES time trace ( $E-E_{0}$ vs $t-t_{0}$ ) of the unoccupied surface and bulk states from Tr-ARPES measurements taken at low excitation fluence ( $15\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro}$ ). We next process the EDC at each delay time in Fig. S13a by subtracting a background that we attribute to dark noise, which specifically includes “hot pixels” in the electron spectrometer, parasitic spectral weight from bands below $E_{F}$ , and pump-induced scatter. Assuming noise from these sources to be independent of delay relative to $t_{0}$ , we compute the subtracted background by averaging each EDC in Fig. S13a over a window of negative delays significantly before the arrival of the pump. In Fig. S13b, we show the resulting the background-subtracted time trace obtained by applying this procedure to the data in Fig. S13a.

There are additionally several other complications that we must overcome in modeling photo-excitation in $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ . First, the unoccupied surface states and the weakly dispersing bulk conduction band below them have significantly different photoemission matrix elements. This is evident from Fig. 2b of the main text, in which the surface states have significantly higher photoemission intensity than the bulk conduction band, despite both sets of states being expected to be occupied under the non-equilibrium conditions of the experiment. The significant difference between the matrix elements of the unoccupied surface states and the weakly dispersing bulk conduction band at ${\bf k}={\bf 0}$ makes it challenging to simultaneously visualize dynamics in the two bands in the raw data. Moreover, completely reproducing the fluence-dependent experimental measurements within a theoretical model of population dynamics solely within the unoccupied surface band would require numerous additional parameters to account for the electronic density of states, thermal band broadening, and the Fermi edge. Even in a simple two-temperature model, we would still be required to fit the numerous additional parameters. Finally, in the most general optical pump-probe measurement of a metal or semiconductor, increasing the pump fluence primarily drives a trivial increase in the electronic occupation of bands above the Fermi level [Chen2018BandPhosphorus], with other – less trivial – observables appearing as secondary effects.

To eliminate contributions from these trivial degrees of freedom, which are not critical to our proposed model of plasmon-driven exciton formation, we next independently normalize the maximum ARPES intensity at each energy level to take a maximum value of 1. The maximum is necessarily reached at $t_{0}$ , up to small energy- and fluence-dependent variation due to rapid intra- and inter-band scattering (see Sec. IV). This normalization of our EDCs allows a complete description of electron population dynamics for low fluence excitation using only two dynamical parameters, as we will shortly detail below in Sec. VIII.2. Beginning with the background-subtracted EDCs for low fluence excitation in Fig. S13b, the Tr-ARPES time trace resulting from this normalization procedure is shown in Fig. S13c. The analogous momentum-integrated raw time trace, background-subtracted time trace, and maximum-normalized trace for high fluence excitation are respectively shown in panels e, f, and g of Fig. S13.

Lastly, we perform a final phase of image processing to visualize the distinction between the unoccupied state occupation dynamics at low and high fluence, In Fig. S13i (Fig. 5b of the main text), we subtract the normalized time trace taken under low fluence excitation from the high fluence analog, resulting in a “normalized difference” trace. We interpret the negative (blue) signal at $E_{CBM}$ in Fig. S13i within the first $2\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$ after photo-excitation as holes associated with exciton formation, given that the negative signal indicates a brief process of significantly faster decay that occurs only after high fluence excitation. We then attribute the relative excess of electrons around $E_{X}\approx E_{0}+$100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ at later delays after high fluence excitation (the broad orange region in Fig. S13i) to electrons of the exciton, as well as to the overall increase in population lifetime due to the weaker effective electron-boson scattering following high fluence excitation. It is important to emphasize that the electrons and holes that contribute to an excitonic bound state are required to have identical temporal profiles [Mori2023Spin-polarizedInsulator]. Below, in Eq. (55) and the surrounding text, we will use a rate equation model to demonstrate how the experimentally obtained normalized difference trace in Fig. S13i is consistent with such electron and hole dynamics.

### VIII.2 Model fitting and discussion

To describe plasmon-driven exciton formation, we introduce a modification of the two-temperature relaxation model [Allen1987TheoryMetals] commonly employed to analyze Tr-ARPES experiments that probe the relaxation of hot electrons via coupling to a cold bosonic bath [Bao2022PopulationCd3As2, Gierz2014Non-equilibriumSpectroscopy, Sun2012DynamicsGraphene]. For sufficiently low energy scales, the dynamics at each fluence can be completely described using two key parameters: an effective electron-boson coupling constant (which acquires a fluence dependence due to screening effects and changes in the initial hot electron bath temperature, see Fig. S10d), and an overall decay constant representing the slow decay of electrons from the unoccupied bands to states below $E_{F}$ via impurity scattering and radiative decay. Beginning with this model, we then introduce plasmon-driven exciton formation as an additional process, superimposed over the thermal decay, that transfers spectral weight from the bulk conduction band towards the higher-energy surface band. We attribute this transferred spectral weight to a bath of long-lived quasiparticles, specifically excitons.

To begin constructing out model, we first note that in experimental ARPES measurements, excitons manifest as electrons near the conduction band when photoemission breaks the electron-hole pairs, accompanied by a dearth of electrons in the effective valence band [Rustagi2018PhotoemissionExcitons, Madeo2020, Karni2022StructureHole, Mori2023Spin-polarizedInsulator]. In our model, we assume that the quasiparticle population dynamics do not strongly influence those of the weakly correlated electrons and holes in the effective conduction and valence bands, respectively. We then note that the onset of the ARPES intensity at the instant of photo-excitation in our experiments is approximately probe-limited ( $200\text{\,}\mathrm{f}\mathrm{s}$ , see the End Matter and Sec. IV). We hence treat the onset of the intensity at photo-excitation as a step function, given that the dynamics described above are significantly slower, and set the observed intensities for both low ( $I_{\ell}(E,t)$ ) and high ( $I_{h}(E,t)$ ) excitation fluences before $t_{0}$ to zero:

$$ I_{\ell}(E,t<t_{0})=I_{h}(E,t<t_{0})=0, $$

where $t_{0}=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$$ .

Next, we describe the electronic population $I^{e}_{F}(E,t)$ at a fluence $F$ (with $F=\ell,h$ respectively for low and high fluences), energy $E$ , and time $t>t_{0}$ using the rate equation:

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}I^{e}_{F}(E,t)}{\mathrm{d}t}=-\bar{\alpha}_{F}(E)\ I^{e}_{F}(E,t), $$

where $\bar{\alpha}_{F}(E)$ is the effective energy-dependent scattering rate. Next, plasmon-mediated hot carrier decay can be described similarly to optical phonon-mediated decay using a two-temperature model [Allen1987TheoryMetals]. In the two-temperature model, $\bar{\alpha}_{F}(E)$ in Eq. (55) is given by [Bao2022PopulationCd3As2, Sun2012DynamicsGraphene]:

$$ \bar{\alpha}_{F}(E)=\alpha_{F}|E-E_{CBM}|+\eta_{F}. $$

## IX Considering alternative explanations of the Tr-ARPES experimental data

In this section, we posit several alternative explanations for our experimental Tr-ARPES observations. We then discuss why each listed scenario is less likely than the mechanism of plasmon-driven exciton formation emphasized throughout this work.

- • The population dynamics follow conventional carrier cooling via bosonic coupling (i.e. a two-temperature model) or electron-electron scattering (Fermi liquid dynamics). This scenario can be excluded, as it does not capture the existence of a local maximum in population lifetime at $E_{X}\approx E_{0}+$100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ , which is evident from the raw data in Fig. 3 of the main text. In this scenario, carrier lifetimes would instead be expected to decrease monotonically with increasing energy.

- • The population dynamics are described by carrier relaxation via bosonic coupling, with the long lifetime at $E_{X}$ originating from light-induced band renormalization shifting the nondispersing bulk conduction band minimum from $E_{CBM}$ to $E_{X}$ . This scenario can be excluded using the data in Fig. S12, which demonstrate the absence of significant band renormalization or time-dependent photovoltage shifts due to pump-induced heating. Specifically, the bottom of the surface conduction band, indicated in Fig. S12 as the minimum in the imaginary self energy (MDC HWHM) at $E_{0}$ , shows negligible temporal fluctuation.

- • The population dynamics follow carrier relaxation via bosonic coupling, with the long lifetime at $E_{X}$ originating from a population bottleneck at the minimum of an unoccupied (topological) surface band $E_{0}$ [Zhu2015UltrafastSb2Te3] (which lies close to a surface Dirac crossing, see Figs. S5 and S6). Bottlenecks lead to a maximum in population lifetime at the bottom (or Dirac point) of a surface band (here $E_{0}$ ), up to broadening effects on the order of tens of meV. However, this scenario is not in agreement with our experimental Tr-ARPES measurements of $\text{EuCd}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{As}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ , in which the bottom of the unoccupied band instead remains well-defined at $E_{0}$ at the same delay times at which a persisting population is observed $100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$ higher, at $E_{X}$ (see for example Fig. S13e,f,g,i).

- • The long-lived population at $E_{X}$ is a consequence of Auger processes, resulting from scattering between electrons in the nondispersing bulk conduction band at $E_{X}-E^{\prime}$ and higher-energy states at $E_{X}+E^{\prime}$ , where $E^{\prime}\approx$200\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}$$ is the energy separation between the persisting population ( $E_{X}$ ) and the identified holes in the bulk conduction band ( $E_{CBM}$ ). This scenario can be excluded, because the electronic states at $E_{X}+E^{\prime}$ are directly probed by our measurements (Fig. 3 of the main text), and instead show short population lifetimes. This indicates that such Auger processes, though not explicitly disallowed, are extremely unlikely at later delays, including past $t_{0}+$1\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$$ . Moreover, the states at $E_{X}+E^{\prime}$ lie distinctly above the energy accessed by optical inter-band transitions, and therefore never become significantly populated.

- • Phonon-mediated scattering from bulk conduction band minima at the $M$ and $L$ points of the Brillouin zone – which are not probed in this experiment – could be (nearly-) degenerate with $E_{X}$ , and could therefore act to create the long lifetime at $E_{X}$ [Jabed2026ControlRenormalization, Fragkos2024Excited1T-ZrTe2]. This scenario can be excluded, because such relaxation processes rely on the presence of a cold phonon bath, and are hence lowest order in the fluence. A model based on phonon-mediated scattering would therefore fail to explain the emergence of the long-lived population at $E_{X}$ at only higher fluences (Fig. S13). Such a model would also fail to capture more subtle features of our experimental observations, including the rapid population decrease at $E_{CBM}$ in Fig. S13i (Fig. 5b of the main text). Lastly, such a model would require discarding the evidence that electronic states are coupled to the bulk plasmon – which is supported by the experimental data in Fig. S11 (Fig. 4a of the main text) – in favor of electron-phonon coupling, for which there is conversely no explicit evidence.

## Abstract

We use momentum-resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy (M-EELS) to study the low-energy charge excitations of 1 $T$ -TaS2 across the nearly commensurate-to–commensurate charge-density-wave (CDW) transition. Single-crystal x-ray diffraction and elastic M-EELS measurements confirm the expected rotation of the CDW wave vector upon entering the commensurate phase. In the nearly commensurate phase, the low-energy M-EELS spectra reveal an acoustic phonon branch and two optical phonon features whose energies and dispersions are broadly consistent with previous calculations and inelastic x-ray measurements. Across the transition, the optical phonon energies remain nearly unchanged, while their spectral intensity develops a pronounced temperature dependence near the CDW ordering wave vector. At higher energies, the finite-momentum charge response undergoes a substantial redistribution of spectral weight below the transition, consistent with the opening of an energy gap. These results demonstrate that M-EELS provides simultaneous access to lattice dynamics and finite-momentum valence band charge excitations in 1 $T$ -TaS2, revealing their evolution across the commensurate CDW transition.

## I Introduction

Charge density waves (CDWs) are a ubiquitous form of broken-symmetry state in correlated electron systems, arising from an intrinsic instability of the electronic structure driven by electron–electron interactions. They have been a subject of sustained interest for decades, most recently because CDW order frequently competes or intertwines with other collective phases, including superconductivity, spin-density-wave order, and electronic nematicity [3, 13]. As a result, CDWs serve as an important model system for understanding how collective electronic degrees of freedom organize in low-dimensional and strongly correlated materials.

Despite decades of study, significant questions remain about the collective dynamics of CDWs, largely due to experimental limitations. The relevant excitations occur at meV energy scales and finite momentum [16, 26], a region of phase space traditionally only accessible with inelastic x-ray and neutron scattering. These techniques are mainly sensitive to phonon excitations [33, 4], so behavior of electronic excitations associated with CDWs has been explored very little.

In recent years, tremendous progress has been made in meV-resolved inelastic electron scattering with high momentum resolution (EELS) [1]. In contrast to neutrons and x-rays, EELS is mainly sensitive to electronic excitations, since the scattering from nuclei and core electrons cancel one another [35, 33]. This attribute of EELS has been used to detect Bose condensation of excitons in TiSe2 [18] as well as a susceptibility divergence near the CDW transition in ErTe3 [5], opening the possibility of studying electronic properties of CDWs more generally.

Among CDW materials, the transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have emerged as canonical systems. A prototypical example is TaS2, which crystallizes in several polytypes, most notably the 1 $T$ and 2 $H$ structures. Of these, 1 $T$ -TaS2 exhibits an exceptionally rich phase diagram characterized by multiple charge-ordered states [28, 26, 34, 27, 19]. Upon cooling, 1 $T$ -TaS2 undergoes a sequence of CDW transitions. An incommensurate CDW phase first develops below approximately 543 K, followed by a nearly commensurate CDW phase below about 352 K. At still lower temperatures, below 183 K, the system undergoes a first-order transition into a fully commensurate CDW phase characterized by a $\sqrt{13}$ × $\sqrt{13}$ superstructure rotated with respect to the underlying lattice [32, 28, 7, 9]. In real space, this reconstruction corresponds to the formation of the well-known Star-of-David clusters, in which thirteen Ta atoms distort cooperatively. The transition from the nearly commensurate to the commensurate CDW phase is first order and is widely believed to be accompanied by a Mott metal–insulator transition. In this picture, Coulomb repulsion among the small number of Ta 5d electrons per reconstructed unit cell—electrons that remain partially ungapped in the nearly commensurate phase—drives localization in the commensurate state [12, 29, 25]. As a result, 1 $T$ -TaS2 provides a rare and compelling platform in which charge order, electronic correlations, and lattice reconstruction are deeply entangled [30].

Reports of the periodicity of the commensurate phase along the c direction are conflicting. Spijkerman et al. reported an ordered stacking with a periodicity corresponding to $L$ =1/3 [30]. In contrast, several earlier diffraction studies found no well-defined periodicity along the $c$ -axis direction, instead observing diffuse scattering over a broad range of $L$ values, indicative of substantial stacking disorder [14, 23, 31].

Previous studies of collective excitations in 1 $T$ -TaS2 have focused primarily on the dispersion of acoustic phonon modes. In inelastic neutron scattering measurements, Ziebeck et al. [36] observed a pronounced phonon softening in the nearly commensurate phase, consistent with a Kohn anomaly at $q\simeq$ 0.27 r.l.u. along the $\Gamma$ -M direction. Using x-ray thermal diffuse scattering, Machida et al. [21] inferred a similar anomaly at $q\simeq$ 0.28 r.l.u. in the high-temperature incommensurate phase; this feature occurs at a different out-of-plane momentum but corresponds to the same in-plane wave vector. More recently, Liu et al. [20] employed inelastic x-ray scattering to directly measure the phonon dispersion and reported an anomaly at $q\simeq$ 0.3 r.l.u. along $\Gamma$ -M, in quantitative agreement with the earlier neutron results in the nearly commensurate phase.

By contrast, considerably less attention has been paid to optical phonons in 1 $T$ -TaS2. Moreover, while lattice excitations provide important insight into electron-phonon coupling, a complete description of the CDW state also requires measurement of the valence band electronic excitations, such as the opening of a CDW-induced gap. Here, we present a study of 1 $T$ -TaS2 using momentum-resolved inelastic electron scattering (M-EELS). A key advantage to the EELS technique is that it is intrinsically more sensitive to charge and electronic collective excitations than either inelastic x-ray or neutron scattering [33, 1, 35], providing detailed insight into the behavior of valence band electronic excitations.

## II Experiment

Single crystals of 1 $T$ -TaS2 were commercially obtained from HQGraphene. In order to assure high crystal quality, the crystal structure and charge-density-wave (CDW) order were characterized using single-crystal x-ray diffraction (XRD) with a Bruker X8ApexII (APEX) instrument. XRD measurements were carried out both above and below the NC–C transition temperature. The results are summarized in Fig. 1, which shows reciprocal-space cuts at different values of the out-of-plane momentum $L$ . Above the transition, the characteristic satellite peaks associated with the NC-CDW are clearly observed, confirming the presence of the NC phase. Upon cooling into the commensurate phase, the expected reorientation of the CDW wave vector is observed, providing an unambiguous structural fingerprint of the NC–C transition.

While the underlying crystal exhibits high three-dimensional structural quality, the CDW satellites are observed over a broad range of $L$ values in both phases. This indicates a lack of long-range coherence of the CDW order along the $c$ -axis and is consistent with significant stacking faults in the CDW order [14, 23, 31]. In one crystal, duplicate reflections, forming an array of twelve satellites around each structural Bragg peak, were observed similar to those reported intermittently in Ref. [8]. In this study, we focus on crystals exhibiting the usual six satellite reflections, as shown in Fig. 1, which constituted the majority of the samples.

For M-EELS measurements, 1 $T$ -TaS2 crystals were mechanically cut into millimeter-scale pieces using a diamond wire saw. Back-reflection Laue diffraction (MWL120) was performed both before and after cutting to verify crystalline quality and to determine the in-plane crystallographic orientation, which was marked on the sample holder. Posts were then glued onto the samples, which were transferred into the UHV system. Samples were cleaved in situ at a base pressure of $5\times 10^{-10}$ Torr and transferred directly into the EELS chamber for measurements.

M-EELS experiments were performed using a custom-built, high-resolution instrument based on a reflection-mode HR-EELS spectrometer equipped with a eucentric five-axis goniometer. The eucentric geometry allows independent, automated control of incident and scattered angles while maintaining a fixed sample position, enabling precise and independent control over the in-plane momentum transfer, $q$ , and the out-of-plane momentum transfer, $q_{z}$ . With M-EELS, the momentum transfer $q$ is held constant while scanning the energy loss. Because the electron wave vector satisfies $k\propto\sqrt{E}$ , inelastic scattering reduces the magnitude $|k_{\mathrm{out}}|$ . To maintain a fixed $q=k_{\mathrm{in}}-k_{\mathrm{out}}$ , the scattering geometry is adjusted during the scan by coordinated rotation of $\theta$ and $2\theta$ . This procedure is not normally implemented in conventional HR-EELS that lack precise centering adjustments and in which the geometry is fixed during energy scans [33, 1, 6].

The instrument was tuned in the direct-beam configuration to optimize the balance between energy resolution, momentum resolution, and beam current, as described previously [6]. Under the tuning conditions used in this work, the energy resolution was $\Delta$ E = 5.9 meV as measured in direct beam conditions (without a sample) and 6.2 meV as determined from the full width at half maximum of the elastic line off the TaS2 crystal. The in-plane momentum resolution was $\Delta$ q = 0.019 Å-1. All measurements were performed in reflection geometry, with momentum transfer oriented within the basal plane of the crystal.

Elastic scattering intensity maps, acquired by performing mesh scans of the momentum coordinates $(H,K)$ at zero energy transfer ( $\omega$ = 0), are shown in Fig. 2. In these maps, the CDW modulation is visible as a well-defined peak at finite momentum. The momentum location of the peak is consistent with the x-ray measurements in the NC phase in Fig. 1.

The CDW reflection is resolution-limited in the transverse direction, i.e., the direction perpendicular to $q$ . In this direction, the momentum width of the peak is comparable to that of the specular reflection measured under identical conditions. This indicates that the observed transverse width is dominated by instrumental resolution rather than intrinsic CDW disorder.

Upon cooling into the commensurate (C) phase, the azimuthal angle of the CDW peak shifts from $\phi$ =12o to 15o. This shift is close to x-ray diffraction measurements on the same sample, which show a shift from 13o to 16o (Fig. 1), and agrees with prior reports in the literature within experimental uncertainty. Further, when cooling into the C phase, the longitudinal momentum width of the CDW reflection was found to sharpen (Fig. 2).

Having established the presence and orientation of the CDW order, we proceed to measure the low-energy collective excitations with an energy resolution of $\Delta$ E = 5.9 meV. We begin by examining the low-energy region ( $-25<E<65$ meV), in which phonon excitations should be visible. Fixed-momentum energy-loss spectra were acquired along the CDW direction ( $\phi=12^{\circ}$ ) in the nearly commensurate phase at T = 300 K.

The results are shown in Fig. 3. Two optical phonons are visible which, at $H\approx 0.07$ r.l.u., have energies of approximately 28 meV and 48 meV (these features are not visible at $H=0$ because of interference from the elastic line). In addition, an acoustic phonon branch emerges from the elastic line and disperses to higher energy with increasing momentum transfer, $q$ .

In order to quantify the phonon dispersions, we fit the EELS spectra at each momentum transfer to a multicomponent model comprising an elastic line, acoustic phonon and two optical phonons. The elastic line was represented by a Gaussian function with a FWHM of 6.2 meV. Following Ref. [17], the acoustic phonon was modeled using a general expression based on time-dependent Landau theory for a scalar mode,

$$ f(A,\mu,\tau,E)=\frac{AE}{E^{2}+\left(\mu E^{2}-\tau^{-1}\right)^{2}}. $$

where $A$ is an amplitude and $\mu$ and $\tau^{-1}$ are inertial and relaxational parameters, respectively. This form captures both propagating and relaxational dynamics and provides a robust description of the acoustic phonon, even when it is not fully resolved from the elastic line. The optical phonons were modeled using the antisymmetrized damped harmonic oscillator (DHO) response function [11],

$$ f(A,E_{0},\Gamma,E)=A\left[\frac{\Gamma}{(E-E_{0})^{2}+\Gamma^{2}}-\frac{\Gamma}{(E+E_{0})^{2}+\Gamma^{2}}\right]. $$

The resulting fits are shown as solid lines in Fig. 3, where the individual spectral components are represented as different colors. The extracted phonon dispersions at $T=300$ K are presented in Fig. 4. In this figure, the dispersions are compared to the density functional theory calculations of Liu et al. [20], who calculated phonon dispersions of TaS2 using first-principles methods that properly incorporate van der Waals interactions. From this comparison we conclude that some of the phonon features observed in the M-EELS spectra likely correspond to multiple excitations that are unresolved in the measurement. Within this interpretation, overall the agreement between the calculation and the measurement is reasonable both in terms of the overall energies and the magnitudes of the dispersions.

Next, we investigated how the spectra change as the material is cooled through the commensurate transition at $T_{\mathrm{C-CDW}}=183$ K, which was shown in Ref. [28] to be first order. For this purpose, we measured M-EELS spectra at five different temperatures, chronologically $T=$ 300 K, 30 K, 100 K, 170 K, then 220 K. The results are shown in Fig. 5 for five different momentum values, including $H=0.233$ , which is close to the CDW wave vector. At lower temperatures, the intensity of the acoustic phonon fell below the detection limit because of the reduced Bose occupation factor. So in this figure we focus on the behavior of the optical phonons. We find the energies of these modes do not change appreciably across the transition. The most significant effect, observed only near the CDW ordering wave vector $H_{\mathrm{CDW}}$ , is an increase in intensity with decreasing temperature. The magnitude of the increase shows some history dependence; the T=300 K data, which was taken out of sequence, does not follow the same trend as the other temperatures. This behavior suggests that optical phonons play a role in the first order commensurate transition. We note that this behavior is quite different from the familiar soft mode scenario characterizing second order structural phase transitions [16].

Finally, we examine the M-EELS spectra over a wider energy range, -20 meV $<\omega<$ 1000 meV to gain a view of the behavior of electronic excitations (Fig. 6). We focus on the behavior near the CDW ordering wave vector, $H=0.233$ for temperatures spanning the commensurate transition. At $T=220$ K, above the transition, the spectra exhibit a continuum of excitations that decay monotonically with increasing energy. Below $T_{\mathrm{C-CDW}}=183$ K, a substantial rearrangement of spectral weight is observed, corresponding to the opening of a gap-like feature with magnitude $2\Delta\sim 300$ meV. This value is consistent with previous estimates of the CDW gap from infrared optics, scanning tunneling microscopy, and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy [26, 29, 10, 24, 15, 2, 22]. We interpret this feature as the opening of a Mott gap associated with the localization of electrons within the star-of-David clusters in the commensurate phase.

## III Conclusion

In summary, we have used momentum-resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy to study low-energy collective charge excitations in 1 $T$ -TaS2 across the nearly commensurate to commensurate CDW transition. X-ray diffraction and elastic M-EELS measurements confirm the expected rotation of the CDW wave vector on cooling, establishing that the cleaved surface probed by M-EELS reflects the bulk CDW transition. In the nearly commensurate phase, the low-energy spectra reveal an acoustic branch together with two optical phonon features whose energies and dispersions are broadly consistent with prior first-principles calculations and inelastic x-ray measurements. Across the commensurate transition, the optical phonon energies remain nearly unchanged, but their spectral weight increases strongly near the CDW wave vector, indicating substantial coupling between these modes and the reconstructed CDW state. At higher energies, the finite-momentum charge response undergoes a pronounced redistribution of spectral weight below the transition temperature, producing a gap-like suppression on the scale of a few hundred meV, consistent with previous reports on the commensurate phase. Together, these results show that M-EELS provides a direct probe of the coupled lattice and charge response of 1 $T$ -TaS2, revealing CDW-coupled phonon excitations at low energy and a gap-like redistribution of spectral weight across the commensurate transition.
